chapman-enskog.title: Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport
chapman-enskog.html:
Chapman–Enskog expansion: from populations to transport

Chapman–Enskog（チャップマン–エンスコッグ）expansion separates kinetic relaxation from slowly varying hydrodynamic fields. The classical kinetic theory is treated by Chapman and Cowling's The Mathematical Theory of Non-Uniform Gases (first edition 1939; third edition 1970). The book's date is not the invention date of the expansion. This chapter gives an independent, unforced, isothermal lattice-BGK derivation at low Mach number.

A small parameter and solvability#

Introduce a bookkeeping parameter ε for slow variation:

fq=fq(0)+ϵfq(1)+ϵ2fq(2)+⋯ ,∂t=ϵ∂t1+ϵ2∂t2,∇=ϵ∇1. f_q=f_q^{(0)}+\epsilon f_q^{(1)}+\epsilon^2 f_q^{(2)}+\cdots, \quad \partial_t=\epsilon\partial_{t_1}+\epsilon^2\partial_{t_2}, \quad \nabla=\epsilon\nabla_1. fq​=fq(0)​+ϵfq(1)​+ϵ2fq(2)​+⋯,∂t​=ϵ∂t1​​+ϵ2∂t2​​,∇=ϵ∇1​.

Conserved moments are carried by the local equilibrium, so higher-order corrections have zero mass and momentum moments:

∑qfq(k)=0,∑qcqfq(k)=0(k≥1). \sum_q f_q^{(k)}=0,\quad \sum_q\boldsymbol c_q f_q^{(k)}=0\quad (k\geq1). q∑​fq(k)​=0,q∑​cq​fq(k)​=0(k≥1).

These are constraints on the expansion, not instructions to erase the nonequilibrium stress. The stress moment of f^(1) produces viscous transport.

Keep the discrete-time Taylor term#

For lattice BGK, expand the streaming side with D_q=∂t+c_q·∇. In lattice time units the Taylor series starts as D_q f_q + D_q² f_q/2. At successive orders,

fq(0)=fqeq,fq(1)=−τD1qfqeq, f_q^{(0)}=f_q^{eq},\qquad f_q^{(1)}=-\tau D_{1q} f_q^{eq}, fq(0)​=fqeq​,fq(1)​=−τD1q​fqeq​,
∂t2fqeq+(1−12τ)D1qfq(1)=−fq(2)τ. \partial_{t_2} f_q^{eq} +\left(1-\frac1{2\tau}\right)D_{1q}f_q^{(1)} =-\frac{f_q^{(2)}}{\tau}. ∂t2​​fqeq​+(1−2τ1​)D1q​fq(1)​=−τfq(2)​​.

The first-order mass and momentum moments give the continuity and Euler parts. The second-order stress correction supplies the Newtonian viscous part. D2Q9 equilibrium isotropy, the low-Mach approximation, and the preceding factor give the shear viscosity

ν=cs2(τ−12)Δt. \nu=c_s^2\left(\tau-\frac12\right)\Delta t. ν=cs2​(τ−21​)Δt.

Here τ is the dimensionless number of lattice time steps used for relaxation, with physical τ_relax=τΔt. Continuous-time BGK instead gives ν=c_s²τ_relax for the corresponding isothermal model; there is no streaming Taylor half-step in that continuous equation. Mixing those definitions yields a wrong viscosity.

What this derivation does and does not establish#

The D2Q9 experiment measures shear damping rather than only substituting this formula. Qian et al. (1992) is the lattice-model source; the BGK source concerns continuous kinetic relaxation. Guo et al. (2002) treats the force discretization separately; the unforced algebra above does not derive its source term.

This is a formal near-equilibrium asymptotic expansion, with small gradients and small Mach number for the truncated isothermal equilibrium. It does not prove stability near shocks, justify arbitrary relaxation times, recover an energy equation, or make this model a general rarefied-gas Boltzmann solver. Burnett-order transport and thermal collision models require additional moments and analysis.

cip.title: CIP: carry the value and the gradient
cip.html:
CIP: carry the value and the gradient

The original cubic-interpolated pseudo-particle (CIP) idea stores a field and its spatial derivative, then reconstructs an upwind cubic profile. The broader family is also called constrained interpolation profile. The CIP notebook implements the original polynomial construction for constant-speed periodic scalar advection. It compares value-only linear interpolation with CIP and checks diffusion, gradient transport, oscillations, refinement, and conservation.

Historical references are Takewaki–Nishiguchi–Yabe (1985) and Yabe–Aoki (1991). The accessible Saito–Obase–Abe-Ouchi (2020) paper describes CIP-family value/gradient evolution and a rational variant; its ice-sheet application and RCIP algorithm are separate from this polynomial example.

Characteristics and an additional unknown#

For constant velocity a,

ft+afx=0,g=fx,gt+agx=0. f_t+a f_x=0,\qquad g=f_x,\qquad g_t+a g_x=0. ft​+afx​=0,g=fx​,gt​+agx​=0.

At a receiving point x_i, trace backward to x_d=x_i−a dt. Interpolate both f and g from the old upwind interval at that departure point. The evolved g is an independent state variable; it is not replaced after each step by a finite difference of the updated f. For N nodes, CIP therefore stores 2N scalar unknowns, while the linear comparison stores N.

For variable velocity the gradient equation instead includes stretching:

gt+agx=−axg. g_t+a g_x=-a_xg. gt​+agx​=−ax​g.

Source terms, velocity variation, and compressibility require additional updates and characteristic treatment. A transported tracer f_t+a f_x=0 and a conserved density f_t+(af)_x=0 also differ when a_x is nonzero. This edition uses constant a only, where the two PDE forms coincide.

Four endpoint constraints determine a cubic#

On an interval of width h, with normalized coordinate s∈[0,1], the cubic is

P(s)=H00(s)fL+hH10(s)gL+H01(s)fR+hH11(s)gR, P(s)=H_{00}(s)f_L+hH_{10}(s)g_L+H_{01}(s)f_R+hH_{11}(s)g_R, P(s)=H00​(s)fL​+hH10​(s)gL​+H01​(s)fR​+hH11​(s)gR​,
H00=2s3−3s2+1,H10=s3−2s2+s,H01=−2s3+3s2,H11=s3−s2. \begin{aligned} H_{00}&=2s^3-3s^2+1,&H_{10}&=s^3-2s^2+s,\\ H_{01}&=-2s^3+3s^2,&H_{11}&=s^3-s^2. \end{aligned} H00​H01​​=2s3−3s2+1,=−2s3+3s2,​H10​H11​​=s3−2s2+s,=s3−s2.​

The endpoint values and physical derivatives are reproduced, and the new states are f_i=P(s_d) and g_i=P′(s_d)/h. Here P′ differentiates with respect to s. For positive a, the interval is [x_{i−1},x_i] and s_d=1−a dt/h; for negative a it is [x_i,x_{i+1}] and s_d=−a dt/h. The implementation restricts |a|dt/h≤1 to keep the departure point in this adjacent interval. The case |a|dt/h=1 shifts both arrays by one node exactly.

This is a complete characteristic/remapping update for this constant-speed problem, rather than a spatial RHS subsequently advanced by an arbitrary RK method. It belongs beside the RK family, not inside its list of time-integration tableaus. More general semi-Lagrangian schemes can cross multiple cells; that capability is outside this adjacent-cell example.

Reproducible scalar tests#

The domain is periodic [0,1], with N=128 point nodes x_i=i/N. Notebook choices are a=±1, Courant magnitudes 0.25, 0.6, or 1, and final times 0.25 or 1. The last step is shortened. Every configuration is solved independently to its selected final time, without interpolation between saved solutions.

The smooth profile is 1+0.2 sin(2πx). Initial g is either its analytic derivative or the centered periodic difference. The square pulse is one on [0.2,0.4) and zero elsewhere. Its initial slopes are either zero or centered differences. Zero is an explicit convention at a sampled discontinuity, not an analytic derivative there. Consequently there is no square-pulse exact gradient error displayed.

The reference f is exact translated point samples. These are not the cell-average references used in the finite-volume limiter notebook. Reported L1 means the average absolute point error. Initial-gradient choice can materially affect sharp features. The basic cubic has no TVD, monotonicity, or positivity limiter, and the square test shows overshoot and undershoot. The linear interpolation comparison is the same signed-characteristic point-value update, algebraically first-order upwind for |C|≤1.

Smooth refinement uses N=32,64,128,256, a=1, Courant=0.6, and T=0.37. The computed value errors approach order three for both gradient initializations; the gradient errors are recorded separately. A cubic interpolant alone is not a fourth-order global-accuracy claim after repeated remapping. Integer Courant shifts are a special exact-translation case, so they are not used to infer a generic refinement order. No equal-cost ranking is made between the N-state linear method and the 2N-state CIP method.

Why a sine wave is not a conservation proof#

The exact integral of the periodic piecewise-Hermite reconstruction is

M=∑i[h2(fi+fi+1)+h212(gi−gi+1)]=h∑ifi. M=\sum_i\left[\frac h2(f_i+f_{i+1})+ \frac{h^2}{12}(g_i-g_{i+1})\right]=h\sum_i f_i. M=i∑​[2h​(fi​+fi+1​)+12h2​(gi​−gi+1​)]=hi∑​fi​.

For uniform constant-speed remapping with fraction s, its one-step change is

ΔM=h2 [H10(s)+H11(s)]∑igi. \Delta M=h^2\,[H_{10}(s)+H_{11}(s)]\sum_i g_i. ΔM=h2[H10​(s)+H11​(s)]i∑​gi​.

The initial analytic sine slopes and centered differences sum to zero, so the displayed scalar runs can conserve this integral to roundoff even though the method has no universal conservative remapping property.

The separate counterexample uses N=32 and a valid periodic C1 Hermite field with f_i=1 and g_i=1 at every node. This is not a constant function: each interval contains a small cubic ripple, and its derivative varies between the nodes. Its exact integral is 1. Exact translation preserves that integral, while one CIP remapping step at C=0.35 gives

s=0.65,ΔM=h s(1−s)(1−2s)=−0.0021328125. s=0.65,\qquad \Delta M=h\,s(1-s)(1-2s)=-0.0021328125. s=0.65,ΔM=hs(1−s)(1−2s)=−0.0021328125.

The plot shows the exact shifted original reconstruction and the reconstructed CIP field over the first four intervals. This is an intentionally constructed grid-scale test of a claimed property, not a prediction of the mass error for every smooth flow. Integrals are evaluated analytically, not by coarse quadrature. Small errors in an easy test cannot establish a stronger guarantee.

Conservative and shape-preserving branches#

CIP–CSL (Yabe et al., 2001) introduces an integral constraint and conservative semi-Lagrangian transport. Rational CIP / RCIP changes the reconstruction, and variants apply additional shape constraints. Conservation and boundedness require their own definitions and tests; neither follows solely from the CIP name.

This edition implements the original 1D cubic only. CIP–CSL2/CSL4, RCIP, fluid advection/non-advection splitting, multidimensional mixed derivatives, and complete compressible or multiphase solvers are reading context. The existing Euler shock-tube solvers retain their documented reconstruction and flux choices.

Reproduce#

from numart.cip import solve_advection, mass_counterexample

wave = solve_advection(profile="sine", speed=-1., cfl=0.6)
pulse = solve_advection(profile="square", gradient="centered")
print(mass_counterexample()["mass_after"])

python scripts/build_cip.py
python scripts/sync_web_content.py

docs/figures/cip.json records 48 paired CIP/linear configurations, derivative arrays, diagnostics, three refinement series, the conservation counterexample, and source hashes. The browser selects these Python-computed results. Tests check exact cubic reconstruction and derivatives, both directions, one-cell shifts, constant preservation, smooth refinement, oscillations, and the analytic mass-change identity.

coordinates-viscosity.title: Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity
coordinates-viscosity.html:
Polar and cylindrical coordinates: tensors and viscosity

The formulas below use physical components in the orthonormal basis (e_r,e_phi,e_z), with cylindrical coordinates (r,phi,z), phi in radians, and r > 0. A planar polar field is obtained by setting u_z = 0 and all z derivatives to zero. Coordinate-basis tensor components have different metric factors; mixing the conventions creates incorrect viscous forces.

For a reference derivation of cylindrical fluid equations, see Richard Fitzpatrick’s lecture notes. This chapter states a general bulk-viscosity convention explicitly and checks it with analytic fields.

Velocity gradient: differentiate the basis too#

Let L_ij = e_i · ((e_j · grad)u). Its rows are velocity components and columns are differentiation directions:

L=(∂rur(∂ϕur−uϕ)/r∂zur∂ruϕ(∂ϕuϕ+ur)/r∂zuϕ∂ruz(∂ϕuz)/r∂zuz). L=\begin{pmatrix} \partial_r u_r & (\partial_\phi u_r-u_\phi)/r & \partial_z u_r\\ \partial_r u_\phi & (\partial_\phi u_\phi+u_r)/r & \partial_z u_\phi\\ \partial_r u_z & (\partial_\phi u_z)/r & \partial_z u_z \end{pmatrix}. L=​∂r​ur​∂r​uϕ​∂r​uz​​(∂ϕ​ur​−uϕ​)/r(∂ϕ​uϕ​+ur​)/r(∂ϕ​uz​)/r​∂z​ur​∂z​uϕ​∂z​uz​​​.

The terms −u_phi/r and +u_r/r arise from rotation of the basis. Define D = (L+L^T)/2 and theta = tr(L):

θ=∇⋅u=∂rur+urr+∂ϕuϕr+∂zuz. \theta=\nabla\cdot u=\partial_r u_r+\frac{u_r}{r} +\frac{\partial_\phi u_\phi}{r}+\partial_z u_z. θ=∇⋅u=∂r​ur​+rur​​+r∂ϕ​uϕ​​+∂z​uz​.

The input partials[...,i,j] in numart.coordinates means the plain coordinate derivative of physical velocity component i with respect to coordinate j = (r,phi,z). Supply the phi derivative itself, not a derivative already divided by r.

Newtonian stress: all six independent components#

With total stress sigma = −p I + tau, dynamic shear viscosity mu, and bulk viscosity zeta, the three-dimensional constitutive law is

τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−23μ. \tau=2\mu D+\lambda\theta I,\qquad \lambda=\zeta-\frac23\mu. τ=2μD+λθI,λ=ζ−32​μ.

Stokes’ hypothesis sets zeta = 0. It is a material assumption, distinct from imposing incompressibility theta = 0. Positive mu and nonnegative zeta ensure nonnegative viscous dissipation.

τrr=2μ ∂rur+λθ,τϕϕ=2μr(ur+∂ϕuϕ)+λθ,τzz=2μ ∂zuz+λθ,τrϕ=μ(∂ruϕ−uϕr+∂ϕurr),τrz=μ(∂zur+∂ruz),τϕz=μ(∂zuϕ+∂ϕuzr). \begin{aligned} \tau_{rr}&=2\mu\,\partial_r u_r+\lambda\theta,\\ \tau_{\phi\phi}&=\frac{2\mu}{r}(u_r+\partial_\phi u_\phi)+\lambda\theta,\\ \tau_{zz}&=2\mu\,\partial_z u_z+\lambda\theta,\\ \tau_{r\phi}&=\mu\left(\partial_r u_\phi-\frac{u_\phi}{r} +\frac{\partial_\phi u_r}{r}\right),\\ \tau_{rz}&=\mu(\partial_z u_r+\partial_r u_z),\\ \tau_{\phi z}&=\mu\left(\partial_z u_\phi+\frac{\partial_\phi u_z}{r}\right). \end{aligned} τrr​τϕϕ​τzz​τrϕ​τrz​τϕz​​=2μ∂r​ur​+λθ,=r2μ​(ur​+∂ϕ​uϕ​)+λθ,=2μ∂z​uz​+λθ,=μ(∂r​uϕ​−ruϕ​​+r∂ϕ​ur​​),=μ(∂z​ur​+∂r​uz​),=μ(∂z​uϕ​+r∂ϕ​uz​​).​

The lower indices here label physical components, not covariant coordinate-basis components. Off-diagonal engineering shear rates are twice the corresponding D component; applying another factor of two to the formulas above would be an error.

Stress divergence: the viscous force per volume#

For a symmetric physical stress tensor, f = div(tau) has components

fr=∂rτrr+1r∂ϕτrϕ+∂zτrz+τrr−τϕϕr,fϕ=∂rτrϕ+1r∂ϕτϕϕ+∂zτϕz+2τrϕr,fz=∂rτrz+1r∂ϕτϕz+∂zτzz+τrzr. \begin{aligned} f_r&=\partial_r\tau_{rr}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{r\phi} +\partial_z\tau_{rz}+\frac{\tau_{rr}-\tau_{\phi\phi}}r,\\ f_\phi&=\partial_r\tau_{r\phi}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{\phi\phi} +\partial_z\tau_{\phi z}+\frac{2\tau_{r\phi}}r,\\ f_z&=\partial_r\tau_{rz}+\frac1r\partial_\phi\tau_{\phi z} +\partial_z\tau_{zz}+\frac{\tau_{rz}}r. \end{aligned} fr​fϕ​fz​​=∂r​τrr​+r1​∂ϕ​τrϕ​+∂z​τrz​+rτrr​−τϕϕ​​,=∂r​τrϕ​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕϕ​+∂z​τϕz​+r2τrϕ​​,=∂r​τrz​+r1​∂ϕ​τϕz​+∂z​τzz​+rτrz​​.​

The acceleration contribution is f/rho. Pressure contributes −grad(p) separately. These divergence formulas allow spatially variable mu and zeta when stress derivatives include their variation. In the Python routine, partials[...,i,j,k] is the coordinate derivative k of physical stress component (i,j).

Constant viscosity and the vector Laplacian#

Only for constant mu and lambda can the force be simplified to

f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ. f=\mu\nabla^2 u+(\mu+\lambda)\nabla\theta. f=μ∇2u+(μ+λ)∇θ.

For a scalar g, let

Δsg=1r∂r(r∂rg)+1r2∂ϕ2g+∂z2g. \Delta_s g=\frac1r\partial_r(r\partial_r g) +\frac1{r^2}\partial_\phi^2g+\partial_z^2g. Δs​g=r1​∂r​(r∂r​g)+r21​∂ϕ2​g+∂z2​g.

The physical components of the vector Laplacian are

(∇2u)r=Δsur−urr2−2r2∂ϕuϕ,(∇2u)ϕ=Δsuϕ−uϕr2+2r2∂ϕur,(∇2u)z=Δsuz. \begin{aligned} (\nabla^2u)_r&=\Delta_su_r-\frac{u_r}{r^2} -\frac2{r^2}\partial_\phi u_\phi,\\ (\nabla^2u)_\phi&=\Delta_su_\phi-\frac{u_\phi}{r^2} +\frac2{r^2}\partial_\phi u_r,\\ (\nabla^2u)_z&=\Delta_su_z. \end{aligned} (∇2u)r​(∇2u)ϕ​(∇2u)z​​=Δs​ur​−r2ur​​−r22​∂ϕ​uϕ​,=Δs​uϕ​−r2uϕ​​+r22​∂ϕ​ur​,=Δs​uz​.​

For incompressible constant-viscosity flow, theta vanishes, but the radial and azimuthal vector-Laplacian metric terms remain. For variable coefficients, pulling mu outside derivatives omits terms 2D·grad(mu) and theta grad(lambda). Evaluate the full stress divergence instead.

Axisymmetry, polar slices, and material acceleration#

Axisymmetry removes phi derivatives, not the terms u_r/r, −u_phi/r, or the stress-divergence metric terms. Axisymmetric flow may still have swirl. For a planar polar slice of a three-dimensional Newtonian fluid, retain the 2mu/3 bulk correction and tau_zz = lambda theta. A genuinely two-dimensional constitutive model uses a different deviatoric trace subtraction and must be declared separately.

The scalar advective derivative is D_s/Dt = partial_t + u_r partial_r + (u_phi/r) partial_phi + u_z partial_z. Vector material acceleration has extra radial and azimuthal terms:

ar=DsurDt−uϕ2r,aϕ=DsuϕDt+uruϕr,az=DsuzDt. a_r=\frac{D_su_r}{Dt}-\frac{u_\phi^2}{r},\qquad a_\phi=\frac{D_su_\phi}{Dt}+\frac{u_ru_\phi}{r},\qquad a_z=\frac{D_su_z}{Dt}. ar​=DtDs​ur​​−ruϕ2​​,aϕ​=DtDs​uϕ​​+rur​uϕ​​,az​=DtDs​uz​​.

These inertial terms are different from viscous metric terms.

Coordinate-basis tensors and transformations#

The cylindrical coordinate basis is (partial_r,partial_phi,partial_z) = (e_r,r e_phi,e_z), with metric diag(1,r²,1). Thus physical u_phi = r u^phi, and physical tau_phi,phi = r² tau^{phi,phi} = tau_{phi,phi}^{coordinate}/r². Covariant, contravariant, and physical arrays cannot be substituted for one another without these factors.

Nonzero Christoffel symbols include Gamma^r_phi,phi = −r and Gamma^phi_r,phi = Gamma^phi_phi,r = 1/r. Covariant differentiation accounts for the same basis changes included explicitly above. The Cartesian transformation uses the orthogonal matrix Q with columns e_r, e_phi, e_z: L_cart = Q L_cyl Q^T and tau_cart = Q tau_cyl Q^T.

Analytic checks and the axis#

  • Rigid rotation: u_phi = Omega r gives antisymmetric L, D = 0, and zero viscous stress. Using partial_r u_phi alone would incorrectly create shear.
  • Pipe Poiseuille flow: u_z = Umax(1−r²/R²) gives tau_rz = −2 mu Umax r/R² and f_z = −4 mu Umax/R². Steady axial momentum requires dp/dz = f_z.
  • Circular Couette flow: u_phi = A r+B/r gives tau_rphi = −2 mu B/r² and zero azimuthal viscous-force divergence away from boundaries.
  • Cartesian affine fields: random constant Cartesian velocity gradients are transformed into cylindrical data and back. Constant Cartesian stresses have zero divergence after angular basis derivatives are included.

The tests also verify the dissipation identity

τ:D=2μDdev:Ddev+ζθ2≥0. \tau:D=2\mu D_{\rm dev}:D_{\rm dev}+\zeta\theta^2\ge0. τ:D=2μDdev​:Ddev​+ζθ2≥0.

These routines require r > 0. At the axis, use regularity and analytic limits rather than replacing r by a small arbitrary number. For a smooth axisymmetric field, u_r and u_phi are O(r), and u_z = u_z(0)+O(r²). Then the axial scalar radial Laplacian tends to 2 partial_r² u_z. Nonaxisymmetric regular Cartesian fields have different component limits; even uniform Cartesian translation need not have u_r = O(r).

import numpy as np
from numart.coordinates import cylindrical_velocity_gradient, newtonian_stress
r, omega = 0.7, 2.0
u = np.array([0., omega*r, 0.])
du = np.zeros((3,3)); du[1,0] = omega
L = cylindrical_velocity_gradient(r, u, du)
assert np.allclose(newtonian_stress(L), 0.)

The code checks tensor identities at supplied points. A cylindrical Navier–Stokes PDE solver, axis boundary scheme, and spherical-coordinate implementation remain future work.

double-mach.title: Double Mach Reflection
double-mach.html:
This chapter records the earlier HLL baseline. A newer lightweight verification compares three grids at the same initial and boundary conditions with a stored finite-grid reference from a separate implementation, including reference-grid sensitivity and unresolved near-wall structure.

Open the additional execution and verification

Double Mach Reflection

This exhibit computes a Mach-10 shock reflecting from a wall using the two-dimensional ideal-gas Euler equations. The benchmark is associated with Woodward and Colella (1984). NASA’s LAVA tutorial is a modern implementation reference.

Equations and initial states#

Use gamma = 1.4 on [0,4] × [0,1], with conserved state U = (rho, rho u, rho v, E) and E = p/(gamma−1) + rho(u²+v²)/2. The initial shock intersects the bottom wall at x = 1/6 and makes a 60-degree angle with it:

xs(y,0)=16+y3. x_s(y,0)=\frac16+\frac{y}{\sqrt3}. xs​(y,0)=61​+3​y​.

The post-shock state to its left is (rho,u,v,p) = (8, 8.25 sqrt(3)/2, −4.125, 116.5). The ambient state to its right is (1.4,0,0,1). The upstream sound speed is one, so the shock-normal propagation speed of ten corresponds to Mach 10.

Initial cell states are assigned by the cell-center side of the shock; cut-cell averages are not integrated exactly.

The moving incident-shock line is

xs(y,t)=16+y+20t3. x_s(y,t)=\frac16+\frac{y+20t}{\sqrt3}. xs​(y,t)=61​+3​y+20t​.

These states satisfy the moving Rankine–Hugoniot relation in the shock-normal direction; the automated check uses normal (sqrt(3)/2,−1/2) and speed 10.

Boundary conditions and discretization#

The left boundary supplies the post-shock state. The right boundary uses zero-gradient outflow. At the bottom, x < 1/6 supplies post-shock data; the remaining wall reflects normal momentum. The top boundary assigns the two states using x_s(1,t). SSPRK2 stages evaluate this boundary at their corresponding stage times.

The calculation uses piecewise-constant finite volumes, a two-wave HLL flux with Davis-type minimum/maximum acoustic speeds, and an unsplit flux divergence. The step is bounded by

Δt=C[max⁡(∣u∣+c)Δx+max⁡(∣v∣+c)Δy]−1. \Delta t=C\left[\frac{\max(|u|+c)}{\Delta x} +\frac{\max(|v|+c)}{\Delta y}\right]^{-1}. Δt=C[Δxmax(∣u∣+c)​+Δymax(∣v∣+c)​]−1.

The displayed run has Nx = 256, Ny = 64, delta x = delta y = 1/64, C = 0.4, final time 0.2, and 811 steps. Its minimum final density is 1.4 and minimum final pressure is 1.0. These are measured diagnostics for this run, not a general positivity theorem.

Reproduce and inspect#

python -m numart.cli run double-mach --n 64 --cfl 0.4 --output outputs/double-mach

Here --n sets Ny and Nx = 4 Ny. The command saves solution.npz, run.json, and double-mach.png. The gallery snapshot includes its run manifest and conserved-state arrays. Array q has shape (Nx,Ny,4); x and y are cell-center coordinates. The manifest records source hashes and the working-tree state at generation time.

What the figure establishes#

The image shows a computed incident/reflected shock pattern, with density and thirty density contours. First-order spatial reconstruction is deliberately diffusive. This grid does not resolve the fine wall jet and roll-up of high-resolution PPM or adaptive calculations. There is no exact final-time solution, grid-convergence study, or digitized original-paper comparison in this exhibit.

Tests check equal-state flux consistency, a periodic uniform state, the incident-shock jump relation, moving-top and reflecting-wall data, and admissible states in a small-grid run. They do not establish convergence of the full reflection pattern. Further work should add higher-order reconstruction, refinement, and independent reference-code comparisons.

For strong-shock instability diagnostics, continue to the carbuncle phenomenon. This HLL image is not a demonstration that a Roe implementation is stable or unstable.

Watch the reflection evolve#

The saved-state movie shows density and pressure from the same 256 × 64 calculation. It includes actual physical times, solver steps, fixed scales, frame inspection, and MP4 export. Read the sampling definitions.

elliptic.title: Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration
elliptic.html:
Diffusion, elliptic equations, boundary conditions, and iteration

Parabolic problems: evolving diffusion#

Solve u_t=νu_xx on [0,1] with zero Dirichlet boundaries and initial data sin(πx). The reference solution is u=exp(-νπ²t)sin(πx). numart.linear.diffusion_1d returns interior nodes.

Second-order centered differences and the θ method give

(I−θνΔtDxx)un+1=(I+(1−θ)νΔtDxx)un. (I-\theta\nu\Delta t D_{xx})u^{n+1} =(I+(1-\theta)\nu\Delta t D_{xx})u^n. (I−θνΔtDxx​)un+1=(I+(1−θ)νΔtDxx​)un.
  • θ=0: FTCS, requiring r=νΔt/h²≤1/2.
  • θ=1: backward Euler, first order in time and unconditionally stable for linear diffusion.
  • θ=1/2: Crank–Nicolson, second order in time and A-stable for linear diffusion.

The Fourier amplification factor is G=[1-4(1-θ)r sin²(ξ/2)]/[1+4θr sin²(ξ/2)]. For large r, Crank–Nicolson can have negative G: high-frequency modes alternate sign while remaining stable. Stability, positivity, monotonicity, and temporal resolution need separate checks. Crank–Nicolson (1947).

spectral_diffusion solves a separate periodic problem by multiplying each Fourier coefficient by exp(-νk²t). Accuracy comparisons with the Dirichlet finite-difference problem must account for their different boundaries.

Thomas elimination: from implicit steps to tridiagonal systems#

For subdiagonal a, diagonal b, and superdiagonal c, forward elimination uses m_i=a_i/b'_{i-1}, b'_i=b_i-m_i c_{i-1}, and d'_i=d_i-m_i d'_{i-1}. Back substitution uses x_i=(d'_i-c_i x_{i+1})/b'_i. Both work and storage are O(N).

thomas preserves its inputs and raises an error for a small pivot. It uses elimination without pivoting, so it is not safe for every tridiagonal matrix. The diffusion matrices used here are strictly diagonally dominant. The original 1949 Thomas report has not been inspected; the historical citation and the verification of this modern implementation are separate claims.

Elliptic problems: the Poisson equation#

The sign convention is -Δu=f. In 1D, use a tridiagonal system and Thomas elimination; in 2D, use a five-point stencil with matrix-free conjugate gradients or multigrid. Default manufactured solutions are sin(πx) in 1D and sin(πx)sin(πy) in 2D. Check the linear-system residual separately from the discretization error relative to the continuous solution.

Dirichlet, Neumann, and Robin boundaries#

Dirichlet specifies u=g_D; Neumann specifies the outward normal derivative ∂u/∂n=g_N; Robin specifies αu+β∂u/∂n=g. The normal derivative is -u_x at the left end and +u_x at the right. Outward conductive heat flux is -k∂u/∂n, so both the specified quantity and its sign matter.

Pass Boundary.dirichlet(value), Boundary.neumann(value), or Boundary(alpha,beta,value) to poisson_boundary_1d. Robin and Neumann conditions eliminate ghost points and use half weights at the endpoints. The time-dependent diffusion_1d currently supports zero Dirichlet boundaries.

A pure-Neumann Poisson solution is determined only up to an additive constant. The divergence theorem requires

∫Ωf dV=−∫∂ΩgN dS. \int_\Omega f\,dV=-\int_{\partial\Omega}g_N\,dS. ∫Ω​fdV=−∫∂Ω​gN​dS.

The implementation checks the discrete compatibility condition corresponding to trapezoidal quadrature and fixes the constant with a prescribed mean, defaulting to zero. Some Robin coefficients also lead to a loss of uniqueness. Periodic Poisson problems similarly need zero-mode compatibility and a mean constraint, with the endpoints identified.

Spectral radius of the iteration matrix#

For a stationary iteration x^{k+1}=T x^k+c solving Ax=b, errors satisfy e^{k+1}=T e^k. In finite dimensions, convergence for every initial error is equivalent to ρ(T)<1, where ρ(T)=max |λ_i(T)|. This differs from the radius of convergence of a power series, R=1/limsup |a_n|^{1/n}, and from a Newton iteration's basin of convergence.

With A=D+L+U, Jacobi has T=-D^{-1}(L+U), Gauss–Seidel has T=-(D+L)^{-1}U, and SOR has T=(D+ωL)^{-1}[(1-ω)D-ωU]. iteration_matrix and spectral_radius support small-matrix demonstrations. Nonnormal matrices can exhibit transient error growth even when ρ<1. The system condition number κ(A) and iteration spectral radius ρ(T) measure different properties. Netlib Templates.

Red-black Gauss–Seidel and SOR#

Color the five-point grid with (i+j) mod 2. Updates of one color depend only on the other color; update red, then black. Set ω=1 for Gauss–Seidel and use 0<ω<2 for SOR relaxation. This interval alone does not guarantee convergence for arbitrary nonsymmetric systems. The implementation targets symmetric positive-definite Dirichlet Poisson problems.

Geometric multigrid V-cycle#

  1. Apply three red-black Gauss–Seidel sweeps on the fine grid.
  2. Compute r_h=f_h-A_h u_h.
  3. Restrict the residual by full weighting.
  4. Solve the coarse-grid error equation recursively.
  5. Prolongate the correction bilinearly.
  6. Apply three more fine-grid sweeps.

Each side has N=2^k-1 interior nodes. Coarse grids use rediscretized five-point operators, and the one-unknown coarsest problem is solved directly. Tests check interpolation, restriction, grid spacing, and boundary consistency. Variable coefficients, anisotropy, curved grids, AMG, and FAS are outside this edition. Fedorenko (1961), Brandt (1977).

For a teaching path, start with Briggs–Henson–McCormick, A Multigrid Tutorial, second edition (2000), then use Trottenberg–Oosterlee–Schüller, Multigrid for local Fourier analysis, algorithm design and advanced applications. The textbook guide explains where each book fits. Their broader scope includes methods beyond the geometric V-cycle implemented here.

Particle and disk gravity#

The new particle-gravity chapter connects PM, P³M, Tree, multipoles, and multigrid. Gravity boundary kernels adds Hockney–Eastwood isolated convolution and Koyama–Ostriker slab Fourier kernels. The existing multigrid example retains its 2D zero-Dirichlet operator; it is not a 3D open-boundary gravity solver.

Further routes to diffusion and elliptic problems#

See continuous P1 FEM for weak-form assembly, GMRES/ILU and nonlinear solves for nonsymmetric systems, and Nishikawa hyperbolic diffusion for auxiliary-gradient pseudo-time iteration. The equation gallery separately shows physical-time heat diffusion.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

Same-system Poisson comparison#

Open the Poisson solver notebook. All 2D methods solve one constant-coefficient five-point SPD system on the unit square with zero Dirichlet boundaries. N=31,63,127 counts interior nodes per side, hence N² unknowns. Every iterative method starts from zero. The common stopping criterion uses the explicitly recomputed true residual, including for CG:

(Ahu)ij=4uij−ui−1,j−ui+1,j−ui,j−1−ui,j+1h2,h=1N+1,∥f−Ahu∥2∥f∥2≤10−8. (A_hu)_{ij}=\frac{4u_{ij}-u_{i-1,j}-u_{i+1,j}-u_{i,j-1}-u_{i,j+1}}{h^2},\quad h=\frac1{N+1},\qquad \frac{\|f-A_hu\|_2}{\|f\|_2}\le 10^{-8}. (Ah​u)ij​=h24uij​−ui−1,j​−ui+1,j​−ui,j−1​−ui,j+1​​,h=N+11​,∥f∥2​∥f−Ah​u∥2​​≤10−8.

Forcing choices are a broad smooth manufactured field and two localized opposite-sign sources. The manufactured solution is u=x(1−x)e^(2x)y(1−y)e^(−1.5y), with f=−Δu differentiated analytically. The localized forcing is 100exp(−[(x−0.28)²+(y−0.35)²]/0.006) −60exp(−[(x−0.70)²+(y−0.65)²]/0.012), with no continuous exact solution supplied. Algebraic error is nodal RMS against the FFT/DST discrete solution; continuous nodal RMS for the manufactured field measures discretization error. Neither is a continuous integral L2 norm. Tight residuals do not remove second-order discretization error.

The separate N=31 single-sine diagnostic uses u=sin(πx)sin(πy) and f=2π²u. It is one eigenvector of this discrete matrix: exact-arithmetic CG requires one iteration from zero. It is therefore unsuitable as the sole general solver benchmark. Broad forcing avoids this shortcut.

The compared configurations are Jacobi, weighted Jacobi (ω=2/3), red-black Gauss–Seidel, red-black SOR, unpreconditioned CG, the existing geometric multigrid V-cycle, DST+Thomas and FFT/DST direct elimination. SOR uses ω=2/[1+sin(π/(N+1))] for this model and ordering. This is not a generally optimal setting for arbitrary meshes/operators. A sweep, CG iteration and V-cycle are different work units. Multigrid has three pre/post RBGS sweeps at every level and additional coarse-grid work. Its cycle count is not a fine-grid sweep count. Netlib's SOR discussion provides the method context.

The FFT route uses an orthonormal DST-I computed with an odd extension and NumPy FFT, following the DST-I definition. The 1D eigenvalues of the difference operator are λk=4h⁻²sin²[kπ/(2(N+1))]; in 2D divide by λk+λl. This solves the same discrete operator, rather than substituting continuum wave numbers k². Zero Dirichlet boundaries are not periodic boundaries. No SciPy dependency is required by the implementation.

Plain Thomas solves 1D tridiagonal systems. The 2D separable direct route transforms y, solves N shifted tridiagonal x systems with Thomas, then applies the inverse transform. It is labeled DST+Thomas, not a generic 2D Thomas solver. Both FFT/DST routes rely on constant coefficients, a rectangular uniform mesh and separable boundary conditions. A separate 1D table compares plain Thomas with FFT/DST at N=63,255,1023 for u=x(1−x)e^(2x).

Timing protocol and downloadable evidence#

Each configuration is run three times after a small N=7 code-path warmup. The reported median trial supplies its own convergence history. Wall time includes solver setup, allocations, per-unit true-residual checks and logging; it excludes imports, problem/reference generation, file I/O and plotting. No cached factorization/eigenvalues are reused between trials. The 1D timings also include their final residual check. Hardware/software metadata and all three times are saved. Python loops and compiled NumPy kernels have different costs; these measurements rank these diagnostic implementations on one host, not algorithms independently of implementation or hardware.

Direct solvers have only a completed-solve endpoint marker. The chart samples long histories and floors displayed residuals at 10⁻¹⁴; full values are in the table and download. The NPZ retains every selected-trial residual/timestamp and final fields. CG's recursive residual chooses directions, but its true residual decides convergence. Residual histories need not be monotone.

Reproduce with python scripts/build_poisson_comparison.py. Download settings, sampled histories, timings and source hashes and fields and full selected histories. Tests independently check DST against a dense sine matrix, direct solves against dense linear systems, common true residuals, all method solutions, zero forcing and manufactured second-order refinement. Variable coefficients, anisotropy, irregular meshes, periodic/pure-Neumann nullspaces and parallel scaling require separate comparisons.

equation-gallery.title: Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm
equation-gallery.html:
Equation gallery: choose the equation before the algorithm

The local Web edition provides an Equations gallery with saved profiles, physical-time controls, fixed plot ranges, initial/boundary conditions, characteristic speeds and links back to methods and papers. It contains nine cases across seven equation families. Data are generated by python scripts/build_equation_gallery.py, not invented animation curves.

Translation and diffusion#

Linear advection u_t+u_x=0 moves a periodic sine wave. First-order upwind with forward Euler is compared with exact translated cell averages. Heat diffusion u_t=0.02u_xx damps the same Fourier mode; centered spatial differences and forward Euler use νΔt/Δx²≤0.4. Their discrete means are conserved.

Burgers: shocks and fans#

Burgers (1948) is the classical model reference; this exhibit uses its inviscid scalar conservation law:

ut+(u2/2)x=0,f′(u)=u. u_t+(u^2/2)_x=0,\qquad f'(u)=u. ut​+(u2/2)x​=0,f′(u)=u.

A decreasing jump forms a shock traveling at (u_L+u_R)/2. An increasing jump forms a rarefaction fan, with u=x/t in coordinates centered on the initial jump. Exact Godunov flux selects the entropy solution, including zero flux inside a transonic Burgers fan. The plotted exact curves are cell integrals, so a shock cutting a cell is not treated as a point sample.

Traffic: a jam can move against the cars#

Lighthill–Whitham (1955) and Richards (1956) are the independent classical traffic references. This exhibit chooses a normalized quadratic fundamental diagram, rather than asserting that every traffic model has it:

ρt+[ρ(1−ρ)]x=0,0≤ρ≤1. \rho_t+[\rho(1-\rho)]_x=0,\qquad 0\leq\rho\leq1. ρt​+[ρ(1−ρ)]x​=0,0≤ρ≤1.

Vehicles move at 1−ρ, while small density disturbances move at 1−2ρ. A jump from 0.3 to 0.9 shocks at speed −0.2, despite positive vehicle speeds. The opposite ordering creates a clearing fan because the flux is concave. Both Burgers and traffic use MUSCL minmod, Godunov flux, SSPRK3 and CFL≤0.4. Density bounds are checked; the solver does not silently clip them.

Fluid systems and kinetic methods#

The existing Euler Sod, wet shallow-water dam-break and isothermal density-jump solvers are connected as additional cases. All three now overlay conserved cell means from semi-analytic Riemann references: known wave fronts split Gauss quadrature, and the 24/48-point difference estimates integration convergence. The reference library explains the formulas, root residuals and point-versus-mean convention. Dry-bed reference formulas do not extend the positive-state numerical solver to dry states. Those models and positive-depth limits are defined in the benchmark guide.

LBM, Chapman–Enskog expansion, periodic incompressible flow, and hyperbolic diffusion have separate computed exhibits. An equation, a kinetic model and a discretization are different choices.

Saved times and reproducibility#

Scalar snapshots observe completed solver steps: their actual times can differ slightly from the requested display times. Output requests leave the trajectory unchanged. The existing 1D system baseline has no snapshot API; its displayed fluid times are explicitly labeled independent solves, each ending at the shown time. Playback links those runs and does not imply identical intermediate steps. Outflow mean changes include boundary flux and are not labeled mass loss.

Download profiles and source hashes. Additional convergence evidence keeps these new experiments separate from the atlas's original validation manifest.

Additional equation maps#

The biological survey catalogs 22 model families with original references and proposed verification, without adding biological simulations. The Arakawa grid chapter adds computed A/B/C Fourier-symbol comparisons for linear rotating shallow water, rather than another fluid movie. These statuses remain distinct from the nine precomputed cases above.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

experiments.title: Interactive experiment guide
experiments.html:
Interactive experiment guide

The basis notebook adds computed reference-element algebra: Legendre and Lagrange shapes, exact versus GLL-quadrature matrices, smooth/jump approximation, and triangular P2 functions. Its saved arrays and source hashes come from scripts/build_basis.py; it does not introduce a new PDE evolution solver.

The web edition now includes a stability laboratory and a convergence notebook. The laboratory computes in the browser; the convergence notebook displays measurements from the original gallery manifest. These are distinct sources of evidence.

Periodic advection in the browser#

The model is

ut+aux=0,x∈[0,1],u(x+1,t)=u(x,t). u_t+a u_x=0,\qquad x\in[0,1],\qquad u(x+1,t)=u(x,t). ut​+aux​=0,x∈[0,1],u(x+1,t)=u(x,t).

Use 64 cell-centered sample points, h=1/64, velocity a=+1 or a=-1, and Δt=|C|h. The signed Courant number is C=aΔt/h. The controls expose 0.05≤|C|≤1.5 and 0–100 time steps. The exact comparison samples the continuous translated profile u(x-at,0) at the same grid points.

Initial data can be a sine wave, a square pulse equal to one on [0.25,0.65) and zero elsewhere, or a sine wave with small high-frequency perturbations:

u(x,0)=sin⁡(2πx)+10−3[sin⁡(2π(N/2)x)+cos⁡(2π(N/4)x)]. u(x,0)=\sin(2\pi x)+10^{-3} \left[\sin(2\pi(N/2)x)+\cos(2\pi(N/4)x)\right]. u(x,0)=sin(2πx)+10−3[sin(2π(N/2)x)+cos(2π(N/4)x)].

The ripple seeds both Nyquist and shorter resolved grid-scale modes. It makes unstable growth visible without relying on machine roundoff. The square pulse illustrates smearing and dispersive oscillations; it is not a smooth convergence test.

Four discrete updates#

numart.advection.difference_step and the browser implement FTCS, upwind, classical Lax–Friedrichs, and Lax–Wendroff. Upwind switches stencil with the velocity sign. The stability chapter develops their context. For FTCS,

ujn+1=ujn−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n),G(θ)=1−iCsin⁡θ. u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n-\frac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n),\qquad G(\theta)=1-iC\sin\theta. ujn+1​=ujn​−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​),G(θ)=1−iCsinθ.

Its squared amplification is 1+C²sin²θ. Consequently, nonzero C produces growing modes even when the necessary domain-of-dependence bound |C|≤1 is met. Upwind, LF, and LW satisfy the Fourier stability criterion for this periodic constant-coefficient problem when |C|≤1.

The solution plot updates alongside |G(θ)|. The reported maximum samples all distinct real-data Fourier wavenumbers of the 64-point grid. The dashed threshold marks |G|=1. When the solution grows, its vertical scale expands rather than clipping the computed values. Pointwise L1 error, maximum amplitude, and arithmetic mean drift are reported separately.

These properties concern this linear periodic model. They do not transfer automatically to nonlinear systems, other boundaries, or a different time integrator. With unstable growth, cancellation and floating-point rounding can also corrupt the measured mean.

Reproducibility and export#

The browser kernels are compared with 24 reference cases generated from the Python implementation: four methods, six signed Courant numbers, and twelve updates per case. Tests compare complete sample arrays and complex Fourier amplification factors. Separate tests check exact one-cell translation at unit CFL, direction reversal, periodic wrapping, and observed-order arithmetic. The fixture records the SHA-256 of numart/advection.py; a source mismatch fails the browser numerical tests until the reference export is refreshed.

The experiment download contains settings, grid coordinates, initial, computed, and exact samples, diagnostics, and the Python reference hash. It records a calculation performed in JavaScript, rather than claiming that Python runs in the browser.

To apply the same stencil from Python:

import numpy as np
from numart.advection import difference_step

n, courant, steps = 64, 0.8, 40
x = (np.arange(n) + 0.5) / n
q = np.sin(2 * np.pi * x)
for _ in range(steps):
    q = difference_step(q, courant, "lax-wendroff")
exact = np.sin(2 * np.pi * (x - courant * steps / n))
print("pointwise L1 error:", np.mean(abs(q - exact)))

Reading a refinement study#

The notebook uses the first-edition docs/figures/validation.json measurements. The original manifest, including source hashes and runtime versions, is available for download. These data predate the browser laboratory and are not new wall-clock measurements.

For successive meshes, the displayed observed order is

pobs=log⁡(Ecoarse/Efine)log⁡(Nfine/Ncoarse). p_{\mathrm{obs}}= \frac{\log(E_{\mathrm{coarse}}/E_{\mathrm{fine}})} {\log(N_{\mathrm{fine}}/N_{\mathrm{coarse}})}. pobs​=log(Nfine​/Ncoarse​)log(Ecoarse​/Efine​)​.

DG advection: periodic scalar transport, final time 0.2, CFL 0.2, N=8,16,32,64, modal Legendre P0/P1/P2, and SSPRK3. The error is RMS sampled at the implementation's quadrature points. It is not a separately integrated L2 norm. Pp stores N(p+1) scalar unknowns. Toggle the horizontal axis between elements and unknowns; the data remain unchanged. Spatial orders 1, 2, and 3 and SSPRK3's time order three explain the expected smooth behavior.

Euler entropy wave: final time 1, CFL 0.3, N=40,80,160, primitive minmod MUSCL or componentwise FD WENO5-JS with SSPRK3. The error is pointwise density L1. WENO's fifth-order spatial reconstruction does not remove the third-order time error, so slopes from this finite sequence do not guarantee asymptotic fifth-order fully discrete convergence. Euler stores three scalar state components per point or cell; equal counts do not imply equal computational cost or identical approximation spaces.

A decreasing error, an observed slope, a positivity test, a small divergence, and a performance comparison answer different questions. The notebook keeps those distinctions explicit. See the benchmark definitions and the implementation roadmap for the remaining checks.

Temporal trajectories and mesh connectivity#

The time integration notebook selects Python-computed y′ = i y trajectories for twelve temporal methods, with fixed final time 20. It exposes step size, leapfrog startup perturbation, two characteristic roots, sampled error, and amplitude. These are precomputed ODE results, unlike the browser-computed spatial stability laboratory. Read the time integration definitions.

The mesh explorer displays three explicit vertex/cell datasets. Selection highlights face-sharing neighbors; the cell dropdown and keyboard-accessible polygons provide equivalent controls. Geometry is fixed, and no flow is integrated. Read mesh definitions, ALE, and SPH.

Both notebooks expose foundations.json, generated by scripts/sync_web_content.py, with source SHA-256 hashes for the temporal and geometry modules. Their Python tests check refinement orders, leapfrog modes, midpoint amplitude, kernel normalization, mesh topology, and moving-volume uniform-state preservation.

Hamiltonian maps#

The Hamiltonian notebook loads 30 Python-computed cases on demand. It compares energy errors at a shared fixed step, then lets readers inspect one map’s phase-space orbit or square-boundary image. Analytic local Jacobian diagnostics distinguish symplectic structure from energy preservation. Read the definitions. Regenerate the dataset and figure with python scripts/build_hamiltonian.py.

Nonsteady movie and KEEP exhibits#

The motion gallery presents actual saved solver states and explicit physical timestamps, with fixed color scales and MP4 export. KEEP is evaluated on a smooth exact-reference vortex, with separate spatial/time-refinement and entropy diagnostics. No shock-capturing claim follows from that smooth computation.

Slope limiters and advanced reconstruction#

The limiter notebook loads 45 Python-computed curves on demand, together with six smooth-refinement studies and three constructed Euler reconstruction failures. Select minmod, Superbee, MC, van Leer, or clipped van Albada, inspect scalar periodic TV and mass, and compare Sod with the same HLLC flux. Scalar errors use exact cell averages; Sod retains its pointwise reference convention. First-order and unlimited baselines apply only to scalar advection.

The advanced controls select TVB M=0,10,50 and demonstrate conservative positive-state scaling. Read slope definitions and the advanced assumptions. python scripts/build_limiters.py generates docs/figures/limiters.json with source hashes; the standard sync copies it to the web edition. Neither the scalar TVB example nor the positive reconstruction helper confers a fully discrete Euler positivity guarantee.

Runge–Kutta family notebook#

The family notebook compares nine fixed-step explicit RK tableaus. Three RK2 methods share a linear stability polynomial but differ on the nonlinear y′=−y² test. Select a one-step size, inspect actual RHS-stage predictors, and compare sampled stability contours and final-time refinement. Formal order, stage count, nonlinear SSP coefficient, and RHS work are displayed separately. Read the RK chapter for all definitions and conditional SSP assumptions. python scripts/build_runge_kutta.py creates the plotted data and source manifest. The existing oscillator notebook now offers twelve temporal methods; its implicit options remain scalar linear models.

CIP value and gradient transport#

The CIP notebook compares original cubic-Hermite CIP with linear point interpolation on uniform periodic scalar advection. It displays the independently transported gradient, derivative-initialization choices, smooth refinement, overshoot on a square pulse, and an analytic conservation counterexample. Read the definitions; point samples and finite-volume averages are not interchangeable. Rebuild with python scripts/build_cip.py before syncing.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

fem.title: Continuous finite elements: from weak form to sparse assembly
fem.html:
Continuous finite elements: from weak form to sparse assembly

Implemented: continuous P1 elements on intervals and affine triangles, Poisson with Dirichlet data, consistent mass matrices, and quadrature error norms. This is distinct from the atlas's discontinuous Galerkin advection example.

The basis-function chapter and notebook connect these nodal shapes to Legendre modes, GLL nodes, exact and quadrature mass matrices, and triangular P2 functions. The assembler in this FEM chapter remains P1.

1943: a variational route#

Courant (1943) is a foundational variational reference. This chapter's small implementation is an independent modern P1 demonstration, rather than a reproduction of his examples.

For −Δu=f, prescribe u=g on the boundary. Multiplication by a test function that vanishes there and integration by parts give

∫Ω∇uh⋅∇vh dΩ=∫Ωfvh dΩ. \int_\Omega \nabla u_h\cdot\nabla v_h\,d\Omega =\int_\Omega f v_h\,d\Omega. ∫Ω​∇uh​⋅∇vh​dΩ=∫Ω​fvh​dΩ.

Write u_h as nodal coefficients times continuous piecewise linear basis functions. On a triangle K, the shape gradients are constant:

KijK=∣K∣∇ϕi⋅∇ϕj,MijK=∣K∣12(1+δij). K^K_{ij}=|K|\nabla\phi_i\cdot\nabla\phi_j, \qquad M^K_{ij}=\frac{|K|}{12}(1+\delta_{ij}). KijK​=∣K∣∇ϕi​⋅∇ϕj​,MijK​=12∣K∣​(1+δij​).

Shared nodes accumulate element contributions into CSR storage. Nonzero Dirichlet values move to the right-hand side before symmetric row/column elimination. Treating only rows would destroy the symmetry relevant to CG. The example uses ILU-preconditioned GMRES.

Inspect the evidence#

The manufactured solution is sin(πx)sin(πy) on the unit square. L2 and H1 seminorm errors are integrated inside elements, not measured only at nodes. The expected smooth-solution orders are two and one. Tests also cover affine patches, nonzero boundary data, constant null vectors before boundary elimination, and total consistent mass.

from numart.fem import poisson_2d
result = poisson_2d(16)
print(result.residual, result.u.shape)

Reproduce with python scripts/build_equation_gallery.py. The dedicated manifest records errors and source hashes. Mixed velocity–pressure elements, inf–sup conditions, curved meshes, general Neumann/Robin assembly and adaptive refinement remain future work. The current projection example uses a staggered finite-difference grid.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

geophysical-grids.title: Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids
geophysical-grids.html:
Spherical meshes and Arakawa A, B and C grids

A/B/C names specify where different variables live on a mesh. They are not an accuracy order, a mesh shape, or a time-stepping family. A structured rectangular mesh may use any of these staggerings. The conventional comparison is described by Arakawa–Lamb (1977), with a useful agency exposition in the ECMWF numerical-methods notes.

Implemented here: spherical mesh geometry diagrams, plus placement diagrams and tested Fourier symbols for a linear periodic f-plane shallow-water system. This is not an A/B/C nonlinear weather or ocean model, and it introduces no new full flow simulation.

A sphere needs several charts#

Mesh geometry and variable staggering are separate choices. A cubed sphere can carry a C-grid arrangement; a triangular mesh can also store edge-normal velocities. A/B/C labels alone do not specify spherical connectivity or metrics.

On a sphere of radius R, with latitude φ and longitude λ,

ds2=R2(dφ2+cos⁡2φ dλ2),Δsλ≃Rcos⁡φ Δλ. ds^2=R^2\left(d\varphi^2+\cos^2\varphi\,d\lambda^2\right), \qquad \Delta s_\lambda\simeq R\cos\varphi\,\Delta\lambda. ds2=R2(dφ2+cos2φdλ2),Δsλ​≃RcosφΔλ.

Geographic poles are regular physical locations. Longitude becomes undefined there, while equal longitude increments become very short near them. An explicit wave/advection CFL bound can therefore become restrictive. Pole filters, reduced grids and spectral methods are other responses; replacing the mesh is not the only option. The three constructions below avoid the single latitude–longitude chart's polar convergence, while introducing other coupling and metric questions. None is automatically equal-area.

Yin–Yang: two overlapping low-latitude patches#

Kageyama–Sato (2004) combine two identical latitude–longitude patches. In each patch's own coordinates,

∣φ∣≤π/4+δ,∣λ∣≤3π/4+δ,xYang=(−100001010)xYin. |\varphi|\leq\pi/4+\delta,\qquad |\lambda|\leq3\pi/4+\delta, \qquad \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{Yang}}= \begin{pmatrix}-1&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&1&0\end{pmatrix} \boldsymbol{x}^{\mathrm{Yin}}. ∣φ∣≤π/4+δ,∣λ∣≤3π/4+δ,xYang=​−100​001​010​​xYin.

The rotation puts each chart's poles inside the other chart's low-latitude region. The figure uses δ=3°; purple marks overlap, not a third patch. Each component retains orthogonal latitude–longitude coordinates and familiar metrics. Boundary data must be transferred through the overlap. Interpolating scalar values alone does not guarantee a globally conservative mass budget; overlap ownership/weights and conservative coupling need explicit design. Velocity components must also rotate between local tangent bases. These transfers are explained here, but no overset transport solver is implemented.

Cubed sphere: six connected panels#

The six-face construction is associated with Ronchi–Iacono–Paolucci (1996). Our diagram chooses equiangular gnomonic coordinates. For an orthonormal face frame with outward normal n and tangent directions e₁,e₂,

x(ξ,η)=R n+tan⁡ξ e1+tan⁡η e2∥n+tan⁡ξ e1+tan⁡η e2∥,−π/4≤ξ,η≤π/4. \boldsymbol{x}(\xi,\eta)=R\, \frac{\boldsymbol{n}+\tan\xi\,\boldsymbol{e}_1+\tan\eta\,\boldsymbol{e}_2} {\left\lVert\boldsymbol{n}+\tan\xi\,\boldsymbol{e}_1+\tan\eta\,\boldsymbol{e}_2\right\rVert}, \qquad -\pi/4\leq\xi,\eta\leq\pi/4. x(ξ,η)=R∥n+tanξe1​+tanηe2​∥n+tanξe1​+tanηe2​​,−π/4≤ξ,η≤π/4.

The picture has 8×8 cells per panel. Adjacent panel boundaries match; three panels meet at each cube corner. This mapping avoids a latitude–longitude pole but is generally nonorthogonal inside a face, and cell areas and metric factors vary. Other cubed-sphere projections have different properties. Neighbor indices, vector components and numerical fluxes must agree across seams. A continuous-looking diagram is not a test of those operators.

Icosahedral triangles and their dual#

Start with 20 triangular faces, split each triangle into four using edge midpoints, and project new vertices radially onto the sphere. At level L,

F=20 4L,E=30 4L,V=10 4L+2,V−E+F=2. F=20\,4^L,\qquad E=30\,4^L,\qquad V=10\,4^L+2, \qquad V-E+F=2. F=204L,E=304L,V=104L+2,V−E+F=2.

Level 2 has 320 triangles, 480 edges and 162 vertices. Twelve vertices have five neighbors; the others have six. Connecting neighboring face centers through shared edge midpoints produces a dual with twelve pentagons and otherwise hexagons. Here the centers are normalized triangle centroids: this is a barycentric dual, not a claim of a Voronoi/Delaunay orthogonal pair. For this unoptimized sample, the largest triangle area is about 1.275 times the smallest, so quasi-uniform does not mean equal-area. The connectivity formulas apply to this regular refinement, not every possible spherical unstructured mesh.

The ICON model description is a useful example of triangular mesh geometry combined with C-type staggering. Our illustration is not the optimized ICON mesh or its dynamical core. Accurate divergence, gradient, vorticity and wave dispersion still depend on compatible discrete operators.

Interfaces, vectors and what the figures verify#

A physical tangent velocity is one vector, even when its components differ between charts. If E_A and E_B have orthonormal tangent basis vectors as columns in one common Cartesian frame, then

v=EAuA=EBuB,uB=EBTEAuA. \boldsymbol{v}=E_A\boldsymbol{u}_A=E_B\boldsymbol{u}_B, \qquad \boldsymbol{u}_B=E_B^{\mathsf T}E_A\boldsymbol{u}_A. v=EA​uA​=EB​uB​,uB​=EBT​EA​uA​.

This formula uses orthonormal physical components. Covariant or contravariant components in nonorthogonal coordinates require the corresponding metric and dual basis. Copying two component arrays across a seam is insufficient. For finite volumes, a shared interface needs the same integrated flux with opposite signs in neighboring cell budgets. Overset grids additionally need a well-defined accounting of overlap; summing both full patches counts some area twice.

The geometry tests check unit radii, matching cube-panel boundary nodes, icosahedral edge incidence and valence, Euler's identity, and total spherical triangle area 4π. A deterministic equal-area sample checks Yin–Yang coverage and overlap; this sampled check is not a formal coverage proof. Reproduce both figures with python scripts/build_spherical_meshes.py; the geometry manifest records construction choices, area statistics and source/artifact hashes. These checks do not establish transport accuracy, seam conservation or geophysical wave convergence. Useful next tests would rotate a smooth tracer across every seam and monitor global mass, then compare balanced shallow-water waves under refinement.

A, B and C specify relative placement#

Take free-surface perturbation η at scalar cell centers (i+1/2,j+1/2), with square cell size Δ. Define u as the x velocity and v as the y velocity.

  • A grid: η, u and v are all at the same center.
  • B grid: η is at the center; both u and v are at vertices (i,j).
  • C grid: η is at the center; u is at x-normal faces (i,j+1/2), and v is at y-normal faces (i+1/2,j).

Choosing vertices rather than centers as the origin reverses some diagram conventions without changing the relative placement. Plot the locations and component directions before comparing array indices between models.

On a C grid, normal face velocities naturally supply cell divergence, and center-to-center scalar differences give face pressure gradients. That is the placement already used by the atlas's periodic MAC projection. The relationship concerns spatial location; MAC and an ocean C-grid dynamical core need not share their Coriolis, advection, boundary or time algorithms. The official MITgcm staggering description shows this face-normal arrangement in three dimensions.

Rotation and gravity waves make the difference visible#

For constant mean depth H and constant Coriolis parameter f,

ut−fv=−gηx,vt+fu=−gηy,ηt+H(ux+vy)=0. u_t-fv=-g\eta_x,\qquad v_t+fu=-g\eta_y, \qquad\eta_t+H(u_x+v_y)=0. ut​−fv=−gηx​,vt​+fu=−gηy​,ηt​+H(ux​+vy​)=0.

The continuum has a zero-frequency geostrophic branch and gravity branches

ω2=f2+c2(k2+ℓ2),c=gH,LD=c/∣f∣. \omega^2=f^2+c^2(k^2+\ell^2),\qquad c=\sqrt{gH},\qquad L_D=c/|f|. ω2=f2+c2(k2+ℓ2),c=gH​,LD​=c/∣f∣.

A discrete dispersion relation depends on the operators and the locations. Here each grid uses centered second-order pressure/divergence; C-grid Coriolis uses the symmetric four-point interpolation between u and v locations. With the physical staggering phases removed, the effective wavenumbers are

A:k~=sin⁡(kΔ)/Δ,ℓ~=sin⁡(ℓΔ)/Δ,fh=f,B:k~=2sin⁡(kΔ/2)cos⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ~=2cos⁡(kΔ/2)sin⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,fh=f,C:k~=2sin⁡(kΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ~=2sin⁡(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,fh=fcos⁡(kΔ/2)cos⁡(ℓΔ/2). \begin{aligned} A:\quad &\widetilde k=\sin(k\Delta)/\Delta, &\widetilde\ell=\sin(\ell\Delta)/\Delta,&\quad f_h=f,\\ B:\quad &\widetilde k=2\sin(k\Delta/2)\cos(\ell\Delta/2)/\Delta, &\widetilde\ell=2\cos(k\Delta/2)\sin(\ell\Delta/2)/\Delta,&\quad f_h=f,\\ C:\quad &\widetilde k=2\sin(k\Delta/2)/\Delta, &\widetilde\ell=2\sin(\ell\Delta/2)/\Delta,&\quad f_h=f\cos(k\Delta/2)\cos(\ell\Delta/2). \end{aligned} A:B:C:​k=sin(kΔ)/Δ,k=2sin(kΔ/2)cos(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,k=2sin(kΔ/2)/Δ,​ℓ=sin(ℓΔ)/Δ,ℓ=2cos(kΔ/2)sin(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,ℓ=2sin(ℓΔ/2)/Δ,​fh​=f,fh​=f,fh​=fcos(kΔ/2)cos(ℓΔ/2).​

The computed baseline has ω_h²=f_h²+c²(k̃²+ℓ̃²). For the energy-scaled state (u,v,cη/H), the full 3×3 Fourier generator is skew-Hermitian: its eigenvalues are 0 and ±iω_h. This is a semi-discrete result. A time integrator can add phase error, damping or instability even when the spatial generator conserves this linear energy.

Checkerboards and an unresolved deformation radius#

A centered A-grid pressure gradient cannot see the shortest alternating height mode in a coordinate direction. The B-grid baseline removes that axis-only null mode but retains a diagonal height checkerboard. The C-grid pressure-gradient/divergence pair couples that mode; however, its simple Coriolis average vanishes at certain shortest waves. These are distinct operator effects, not one universal checkerboard diagnosis.

The figure compares both axial and diagonal waves at L_D/Δ=0.25 and 2. A and B overlap on the diagonal for these square-grid operators, while their axial curves differ. When the deformation radius is unresolved, Coriolis averaging can strongly distort the C-grid near-inertial branches. Thus “C is always best” is not a valid conclusion. Resolved gravity waves, coarse-grid geostrophic adjustment and directional errors are different tests. Different Coriolis discretizations can change the comparison without changing the C placement itself.

D and E, vertical staggering and magnetic grids#

The D grid interchanges the face locations of u and v relative to C: u lies at the y-normal face location and v at the x-normal face location. The arrows still denote physical x and y components, so a D diagram is not obtained by merely renaming the C velocity arrays. The E grid is commonly viewed as a B arrangement rotated by 45 degrees; its indexing and resolvable wavevector set must be treated consistently. They are described here but have no implemented symbols in this addition.

Horizontal Arakawa staggering is separate from Lorenz versus Charney–Phillips vertical staggering. Likewise, MHD constrained transport uses face/edge placement to enforce a magnetic-divergence identity; it is not synonymous with an Arakawa C-grid shallow-water algorithm. Each needs its own compatible discrete operators.

Evidence and the next geophysical benchmarks#

numart.geophysical_grids supplies the A/B/C symbols. Tests compare them with independently applied physical-grid finite-difference stencils on Fourier waves, check skew-Hermitian energy structure and the geostrophic zero branch, verify long-wave second-order convergence, and expose the distinct short-wave null modes. Reproduce the figure with python scripts/build_geophysical_grids.py; the manifest records assumptions, sampled frequencies and source hashes.

A sensible next flow sequence is geostrophic adjustment, inertia–gravity waves, a coastal Kelvin wave, and a beta-plane Rossby wave, followed by potential-vorticity and nonlinear energy/enstrophy budgets. The present constant-f symbols do not verify beta-plane Rossby propagation, coastlines, spherical metrics, topography or wetting/drying. A nonlinear Arakawa Jacobian or energy/enstrophy-conserving shallow-water flux is another algorithmic choice; selecting A, B or C placement alone does not provide those invariants.

gravity-boundaries.title: Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab
gravity-boundaries.html:
Gravity kernels: isolated FFTs and a periodic slab

The boundary condition is part of a Poisson solver’s definition. A finite isolated mass, a fully periodic density contrast, and a horizontally periodic disk with vacuum above and below have different Green functions. Padding an array does not by itself choose the right one.

The isolated construction here follows the Hockney–Eastwood doubled-domain convolution idea in Computer Simulation Using Particles. The disk reference is Koyama and Ostriker (2009), ApJ 693, 1316–1345, §2.3 and Appendix A (author preprint). It uses horizontal periodicity, vertical domain doubling, and mode-dependent image corrections. Below we derive and test kernels with our own explicit transform normalization; the finite sampled DFT and the continuum Fourier coefficient are distinguished.

Isolated gravity: linear convolution on a doubled grid#

With G = 1, the three-dimensional isolated potential is

ϕ(x)=−∫ρ(x′)∣x−x′∣ d3x′. \phi(\boldsymbol x)=-\int\frac{\rho(\boldsymbol x')}{|\boldsymbol x-\boldsymbol x'|}\,d^3x'. ϕ(x)=−∫∣x−x′∣ρ(x′)​d3x′.

For a source grid Nx × Ny × Nz, pad the density with zeros to 2Nx × 2Ny × 2Nz. Build a kernel using signed grid lags on that doubled domain, multiply its FFT by the padded density FFT, invert, and retain the original physical block:

ϕphysical=ΔV R IFFT⁡[FFT⁡(ρpadded)FFT⁡(Kdoubled)]. \phi_{\rm physical}=\Delta V\, \mathcal R\,\operatorname{IFFT}\bigl[ \operatorname{FFT}(\rho_{\rm padded})\operatorname{FFT}(K_{\rm doubled})\bigr]. ϕphysical​=ΔVRIFFT[FFT(ρpadded​)FFT(Kdoubled​)].

Source–target separations inside the retained block are less than the original domain length in each direction. The doubled cyclic convolution therefore equals the desired nonperiodic discrete convolution. This is stronger than merely moving periodic images farther away. Replacing K by the usual periodic symbol −4 pi/k² would solve a different problem.

The singular grid-origin kernel must be declared. isolated_potential assigns an explicit self_kernel, default zero, and uses −1/r elsewhere. It does not integrate the kernel over a finite source cell. Its roundoff-level agreement with a direct grid sum verifies convolution and padding, not high-order continuum accuracy or a uniquely correct self-cell prescription. A fully isolated finite mass can have phi tending to zero at infinity; a slab with nonzero surface density generally cannot.

Horizontal Fourier transform of a slab#

Take x and y periodic and let the density vanish outside a vertical interval of length Lz. With horizontal wavevector k_perp, use the convention

ρ^k(z)=1LxLy∫ρ(x,y,z)e−i(kxx+kyy) dx dy,k=kx2+ky2. \widehat\rho_{\boldsymbol k}(z)=\frac1{L_xL_y} \int\rho(x,y,z)e^{-i(k_xx+k_yy)}\,dx\,dy,\qquad k=\sqrt{k_x^2+k_y^2}. ρ​k​(z)=Lx​Ly​1​∫ρ(x,y,z)e−i(kx​x+ky​y)dxdy,k=kx2​+ky2​​.

Poisson’s equation becomes (partial_z²−k²) phi_hat = 4 pi G rho_hat. The full gravitational kernel, including 4 pi G, is

Gk(s)={−2πGke−k∣s∣,k>0,2πG∣s∣,k=0,ϕ^k(z)=∫Gk(z−z′)ρ^k(z′) dz′. \mathcal G_k(s)=\begin{cases} -\dfrac{2\pi G}{k}e^{-k|s|},&k>0,\\ 2\pi G|s|,&k=0, \end{cases}\qquad \widehat\phi_{\boldsymbol k}(z)=\int\mathcal G_k(z-z')\widehat\rho_{\boldsymbol k}(z')\,dz'. Gk​(s)=⎩⎨⎧​−k2πG​e−k∣s∣,2πG∣s∣,​k>0,k=0,​ϕ​k​(z)=∫Gk​(z−z′)ρ​k​(z′)dz′.

Our sign convention includes the gravitational prefactor in the kernel; some references factor it out. The derivative jump at s = 0 gives 4 pi G, which checks both sign and normalization. Nonzero horizontal modes decay into the exterior. The zero mode is the horizontally averaged mass sheet, with a finite exterior force rather than a decaying potential.

The vertical Fourier coefficient and the image factor#

Only separations |s| < Lz are required. Extend the kernel periodically over a separation interval of length 2Lz and set k_z,ell = pi ell/Lz. For k > 0 the continuous integral is

G~k,ℓ=∫−LzLzGk(s)e−ikz,ℓs ds=−4πGk2+kz,ℓ2[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz]. \widetilde{\mathcal G}_{k,\ell} =\int_{-L_z}^{L_z}\mathcal G_k(s)e^{-ik_{z,\ell}s}\,ds =-\frac{4\pi G}{k^2+k_{z,\ell}^2} \left[1-(-1)^\ell e^{-kL_z}\right]. G​k,ℓ​=∫−Lz​Lz​​Gk​(s)e−ikz,ℓ​sds=−k2+kz,ℓ2​4πG​[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz​].

It follows by integrating the even exponential against a cosine. The square-bracket factor distinguishes the slab kernel from the ordinary fully periodic Poisson multiplier. Equivalently, doubling z and adding a negative image density at displacement Lz with horizontal-mode factor exp(−k Lz) produces this factor before applying the ordinary nonzero Poisson multiplier.

For the k = 0 horizontal mode, the continuous coefficient is

G~0,ℓ={2πGLz2,ℓ=0,4πG[(−1)ℓ−1]kz,ℓ2,ℓ≠0. \widetilde{\mathcal G}_{0,\ell}= \begin{cases} 2\pi G L_z^2,&\ell=0,\\ \dfrac{4\pi G[(-1)^\ell-1]}{k_{z,\ell}^2},&\ell\ne0. \end{cases} G​0,ℓ​=⎩⎨⎧​2πGLz2​,kz,ℓ2​4πG[(−1)ℓ−1]​,​ℓ=0,ℓ=0.​

The all-zero coefficient fixes an additive potential constant in this convention. Other constant gauges give the same force. Dropping the entire horizontal k = 0 mode, however, removes the physical mean sheet and is incorrect. Our slab solver does not subtract the mean density.

A sampled DFT is a different numerical object#

Let dz = Lz/Nz and s_j be the 2Nz signed vertical lags. The multiplier for the discrete quadrature is

G~k,ℓsampled=Δz∑j=02Nz−1Gk(sj)e−2πijℓ/(2Nz). \widetilde{\mathcal G}^{\rm sampled}_{k,\ell} =\Delta z\sum_{j=0}^{2N_z-1}\mathcal G_k(s_j) e^{-2\pi i j\ell/(2N_z)}. G​k,ℓsampled​=Δzj=0∑2Nz​−1​Gk​(sj​)e−2πijℓ/(2Nz​).

This is exactly dz times the DFT of the sampled kernel. It is not, at finite Nz, identical to the continuous integral above. For k > 0 its real value can also be evaluated by the geometric series

G~k,ℓsampled=−2πGΔzksinh⁡(kΔz)cosh⁡(kΔz)−cos⁡(πℓ/Nz)[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz]. \widetilde{\mathcal G}^{\rm sampled}_{k,\ell} =-\frac{2\pi G\Delta z}{k} \frac{\sinh(k\Delta z)}{\cosh(k\Delta z)-\cos(\pi\ell/N_z)} \left[1-(-1)^\ell e^{-kL_z}\right]. G​k,ℓsampled​=−k2πGΔz​cosh(kΔz)−cos(πℓ/Nz​)sinh(kΔz)​[1−(−1)ℓe−kLz​].

Use a separate k = 0 branch to avoid cancellation and division by zero. Expanding sinh, cosh, and cos recovers the continuous coefficient for fixed resolved modes as dz tends to zero. Tests measure this convergence. The distinction prevents labeling a continuum coefficient as the exact finite sum of sampled values.

slab_green_transform exposes both sampled and continuum representations. slab_potential defaults to the sampled kernel, so its FFT result matches an independent direct vertical quadrature. The continuum option applies the analytic coefficient instead. This is a small independently written kernel laboratory, not a reproduction of all numerical choices or the interstellar-medium simulations in the paper.

Check the boundary physics before a galaxy calculation#

import numpy as np
from numart.gravity_boundaries import isolated_potential, slab_potential
rho = np.ones((8,8,16))
phi_slab = slab_potential(rho)  # horizontal mean mode retained
phi_isolated = isolated_potential(rho, spacing=(1/8,1/8,1/16))

These two arrays describe different boundary problems. Tests compare isolated FFT convolution with a direct nonperiodic grid sum, including a source near a boundary; verify the mean plane’s quadratic potential and linear interior acceleration; and recover the exponential field of a sinusoidal sheet. For a sheet of surface density Sigma, the mean potential is 2 pi G Sigma |z−z0| and the nonzero mode decays as exp(−k|z−z0|).

The kernel verification manifest records source hashes and measured errors for the displayed checks.

The implementation uses ordinary horizontal periodicity, not shear-periodic remapping. Mass assignment, self-cell integration, vertical quadrature accuracy, force differentiation, and gravity–hydrodynamics coupling require further checks before production use. Continue with particle gravity, multigrid, and Hamiltonian maps.
