shock-expansion.title: Traced PPM, AUSM variants and curved bow shocks
shock-expansion.html:
Traced PPM, AUSM variants and curved bow shocks

Open the new computed comparison. This stage adds a direct-Eulerian characteristic-traced PPM update, specified AUSM+ and AUSM+-up fluxes, and a circular-cylinder forebody diagnostic. The earlier method-of-lines reconstruction and planar odd–even experiment retain their original data and scope.

Direct-Eulerian PPM and independent switches#

numart.ppm_traced reconstructs primitive density, velocity and pressure from conserved cell means. It uses MC-limited parabolic interpolation, optional density contact steepening, optional shock flattening and componentwise parabolic monotonicity constraints. Mean conserved states are updated by a shared face flux. A primitive profile reconstructed from a conserved mean is a second-order representation; it is not an exact average of primitive variables.

For each primitive profile, with local cell coordinate xi in [0,1],

q(ξ)=qL+ξ[Δq+q6(1−ξ)],Δq=qR−qL,q6=6qi−3(qL+qR). q(\xi)=q_L+\xi[\Delta q+q_6(1-\xi)],\qquad \Delta q=q_R-q_L,\qquad q_6=6q_i-3(q_L+q_R). q(ξ)=qL​+ξ[Δq+q6​(1−ξ)],Δq=qR​−qL​,q6​=6qi​−3(qL​+qR​).

Average over a fraction sigma of the domain next to either edge:

IR(σ)=qR−σ2[Δq−(1−2σ3)q6],IL(σ)=qL+σ2[Δq+(1−2σ3)q6]. I_R(\sigma)=q_R-\frac{\sigma}{2}\left[\Delta q-\left(1-\frac{2\sigma}{3}\right)q_6\right],\qquad I_L(\sigma)=q_L+\frac{\sigma}{2}\left[\Delta q+\left(1-\frac{2\sigma}{3}\right)q_6\right]. IR​(σ)=qR​−2σ​[Δq−(1−32σ​)q6​],IL​(σ)=qL​+2σ​[Δq+(1−32σ​)q6​].

The three wave speeds are u−c, u and u+c. For each incoming family, sigma=|lambda| dt/dx. Starting from the fastest incoming wave's domain average, correct the other incoming characteristic components using a primitive eigenbasis frozen at the cell state. These are time-averaged Riemann inputs for one conservative step. Applying an additional SSPRK3 wrapper to this predictor would define a different method. The default flux is HLLC and CFL is 0.4.

The construction follows the direct-Eulerian characteristic-domain approach in the inspected Colella–Woodward author preprint, with the 1984 paper as the original publication. The Cholla author manuscript, Appendix A is an additional algorithmic cross-check. The implementation is independent: it does not reproduce every production-code option, multidimensional CTU, artificial viscosity, Lagrangian evolution or remap. Some displayed Cholla appendix signs/indices are inconsistent with the described neighboring-cell construction; the explicit formulas below and executable checks define this variant.

Contact steepening and shock flattening#

Steepening changes density edges only. Let D2_i=(rho_(i+1)−2rho_i+rho_(i−1))/6. Require D2_(i−1) D2_(i+1)<0, a relative density jump above 0.01, and a relative pressure jump smaller than 0.1 gamma times the relative density jump. Then

η~i=−Di+12−Di−12ρi+1−ρi−1,ηi=clip⁡ ⁣(20(η~i−0.05),0,1). \widetilde\eta_i=-\frac{D^2_{i+1}-D^2_{i-1}}{\rho_{i+1}-\rho_{i-1}},\qquad \eta_i=\operatorname{clip}\!\left(20(\widetilde\eta_i-0.05),0,1\right). η​i​=−ρi+1​−ρi−1​Di+12​−Di−12​​,ηi​=clip(20(η​i​−0.05),0,1).

Blend the density left edge toward rho_(i−1)+delta_rho_(i−1)/2 and the right edge toward rho_(i+1)−delta_rho_(i+1)/2, using MC slopes in those neighboring cells. This suppresses contact spreading but can sharpen an under-resolved smooth density transition. It should not be treated as a universal accuracy improvement.

Flattening uses S_i=(p_(i+1)−p_(i−1))/(p_(i+2)−p_(i−2)). The preliminary coefficient is clip(10(S_i−0.75),0,1), enabled only for a relative pressure jump at least 1/3 and a compressive velocity difference. Take the larger coefficient of the cell and its lower-pressure neighbor. Every primitive edge is blended toward its cell value before monotonicity enforcement. A coefficient of 1 removes the spatial variation; 0 leaves it unchanged.

Reconstructed inputs that violate density/pressure thresholds of 1e−12 use a common conservative affine scaling about the unchanged cell mean. Invalid completed updates retry with half the time step, up to 14 attempts. These are safeguards, not a fully discrete positivity proof. Failure preserves the last accepted state and actual time. No state clipping, hidden flux substitution or false final-time label is used.

The four switch combinations use identical flux, nominal CFL and update algorithm. At N=200 for one moving-contact crossing, steepening reduces density error while pressure and velocity stay constant to roundoff. Smooth entropy-wave grids N=32,64,128 show approximately second-order convergence of the complete traced method; no third- or fourth-order time-accuracy claim is made.

AUSM+ and AUSM+-up with stated controls#

The older arithmetic-sound-speed AUSM baseline stays separate. The new fluxes use fourth-degree Mach and fifth-degree pressure splitting. For |M|<1,

M4±(M)=±[(M±1)24+(M2−1)28],P5±(M)=(M±1)2(2∓M)4±αM(M2−1)2. \mathcal M_4^\pm(M)=\pm\left[\frac{(M\pm1)^2}{4}+\frac{(M^2-1)^2}{8}\right],\qquad \mathcal P_5^\pm(M)=\frac{(M\pm1)^2(2\mp M)}4\pm\alpha M(M^2-1)^2. M4±​(M)=±[4(M±1)2​+8(M2−1)2​],P5±​(M)=4(M±1)2(2∓M)​±αM(M2−1)2.

Outside this interval, use signed upwind Mach and pressure fractions. Both variants use the directional critical-enthalpy sound speed employed in the 2006 formulation:

a∗,k2=2(γ−1)γ+1Hk,af=min⁡(a∗,L2max⁡(a∗,L,uL),a∗,R2max⁡(a∗,R,−uR)). a_{*,k}^2=\frac{2(\gamma-1)}{\gamma+1}H_k,\qquad a_f=\min\left(\frac{a_{*,L}^2}{\max(a_{*,L},u_L)}, \frac{a_{*,R}^2}{\max(a_{*,R},-u_R)}\right). a∗,k2​=γ+12(γ−1)​Hk​,af​=min(max(a∗,L​,uL​)a∗,L2​​,max(a∗,R​,−uR​)a∗,R2​​).

The displayed AUSM+ has alpha=3/16 and no pressure/velocity diffusion terms. It is the specified basic member of this formulation, not a claim to reproduce every 1996 interface-sound-speed option. AUSM+-up uses Kp=0.25, Ku=0.75, sigma=1 and a reference Mach cutoff of 0.1:

M‾2=ML2+MR22,M0=min⁡(1,max⁡(M‾2,Mref2)),fa=M0(2−M0),α=316(5fa2−4). \overline M^2=\frac{M_L^2+M_R^2}{2},\quad M_0=\sqrt{\min(1,\max(\overline M^2,M_{\rm ref}^2))},\quad f_a=M_0(2-M_0),\quad\alpha=\frac{3}{16}(5f_a^2-4). M2=2ML2​+MR2​​,M0​=min(1,max(M2,Mref2​))​,fa​=M0​(2−M0​),α=163​(5fa2​−4).

Add the pressure diffusion term to the interface Mach number and velocity diffusion to its pressure:

Mp=−Kpfamax⁡(1−M‾2,0)pR−pLρ‾af2,pu=−KufaP5+(ML)P5−(MR)(ρL+ρR)af(uR−uL). M_p=-\frac{K_p}{f_a}\max(1-\overline M^2,0) \frac{p_R-p_L}{\overline\rho a_f^2},\qquad p_u=-K_u f_a\mathcal P_5^+(M_L)\mathcal P_5^-(M_R) (\rho_L+\rho_R)a_f(u_R-u_L). Mp​=−fa​Kp​​max(1−M2,0)ρ​af2​pR​−pL​​,pu​=−Ku​fa​P5+​(ML​)P5−​(MR​)(ρL​+ρR​)af​(uR​−uL​).

Upwind density, velocity and total enthalpy using the resulting mass-flux sign. Add interface pressure to normal momentum. Tests check uniform flow, both supersonic directions, contacts, stationary normal shocks, sonic branch limits, reversal conservation and rotational covariance.

Liou (1996) and Liou (2006) are the original references. The sound-speed and diffusion definitions were cross-checked against the official SU2 implementation. Our Python code is independent and supplies no implicit Jacobian or time preconditioning.

The low-Mach graph varies the cutoff across 0.01,0.1,1 for a tiny fixed pressure jump. It is a flux sensitivity, not verification of a low-Mach vortex, boundary layer or asymptotic-preserving PDE scheme. A cutoff and the time-step restriction remain part of the numerical method.

Matched one-dimensional problems and a recorded failure#

All new 1D runs use traced PPM with CFL 0.4. The flux comparison fixes contact steepening off and shock flattening on. It switches HLLC, old AUSM, AUSM+ and AUSM+-up. These are independent adaptive-CFL runs, not matched-step or matched-cost timings.

The cases are Sod N=200, moving contact N=200, Shu–Osher N=240, and a strong pressure jump N=200. The first three retain the setups in the earlier comparison. The last uses primitive left (1,0,1000), right (1,0,0.01), gamma=1.4, a jump at x=0.5, extrapolated ends and t=0.01 on [0,1]. Its waves remain away from the boundaries at that time.

Sod and strong-jump density errors use front-split 24/48-point quadrature of conserved Riemann states. The moving-contact reference returns to its initial cell means after one crossing. Shu–Osher retains the earlier internal characteristic FD WENO-Z N=960 reference; it is numerical, not exact, and no exact error is reported. Point-reference curves and primitive variables of conserved means have distinct conventions.

The stated strong-jump AUSM+ configuration exhausts its admissibility retries before t=0.01. Its table reports failure and the actual stopping time; it is excluded from the final-time curves. The download retains the last accepted conserved state and reason. This demonstrates that the implemented flux, reconstruction safeguards and nominal CFL together do not establish update positivity. Other completed runs can also require retries; inspect their counts.

A conservative mesh around the cylinder nose#

The 2D experiment covers only the upstream half of a unit circular cylinder: r in [1,4], theta in [pi/2,3pi/2], with flow in the positive x direction. Straight-sided annular quadrilaterals conform to the polygonal approximation of the body. Two grids have 24×48 and 48×96 cells. Radius and angle are uniformly spaced, but physical cells are not squares.

Cartesian conserved variables use face-normal numerical fluxes with shared face lengths. Polygon areas, radial chord normals and angular-face normals obey geometric closure to roundoff. This avoids curvilinear momentum source terms. Tests check free-stream preservation when the wall is disabled, reflection of wall-normal momentum, zero wall mass/energy flux and the integrated flux budget.

Use rho_inf=1.4, p_inf=1, u_inf=6, v_inf=0, gamma=1.4, giving sound speed 1 and Mach 6. The inner wall is inviscid slip; the outer boundary is fixed free stream and both angular exits extrapolate. Initial conditions are free stream, optionally modified by

ρ(r,θ)=ρ∞[1+ϵe−((r−1.5)/0.3)2sin⁡(12(θ−π))],ϵ∈{0,10−4}. \rho(r,\theta)=\rho_\infty\left[1+\epsilon e^{-((r-1.5)/0.3)^2}\sin\bigl(12(\theta-\pi)\bigr)\right],\qquad \epsilon\in\{0,10^{-4}\}. ρ(r,θ)=ρ∞​[1+ϵe−((r−1.5)/0.3)2sin(12(θ−π))],ϵ∈{0,10−4}.

Velocity and pressure are unchanged initially. The perturbation is a density mode, not a displaced mesh or shock front. The angular wavelength is held fixed under refinement. Both controls and seeded runs use first-order geometric FV, SSPRK2, CFL 0.4 and terminal time 2. CFL uses the sum of all face spectral radii; it is not numerically identical to the 1D CFL rule. There are 20 forebody runs: five fluxes, two grids and two seed amplitudes.

Directional HLLE and Roe composition#

For a face normal n, choose n1 along the velocity jump and n2 perpendicular to it; orient their signs to make alpha_k=n dot n_k nonnegative. If the velocity jump is below 1e−10 in these nondimensional units, n1 is face-tangential and n2 face-normal. Define

F^(n)=α1F^HLLE(n1)+α2F^Roe(n2),n=α1n1+α2n2. \widehat{\boldsymbol F}(\boldsymbol n)= \alpha_1\widehat{\boldsymbol F}_{\rm HLLE}(\boldsymbol n_1)+ \alpha_2\widehat{\boldsymbol F}_{\rm Roe}(\boldsymbol n_2),\qquad \boldsymbol n=\alpha_1\boldsymbol n_1+\alpha_2\boldsymbol n_2. F(n)=α1​FHLLE​(n1​)+α2​FRoe​(n2​),n=α1​n1​+α2​n2​.

The same left/right physical states are rotated into each local frame. Rotate momentum fluxes back to Cartesian coordinates before combining. A normal velocity jump selects HLLE; a purely tangential shear selects Roe in the face-normal direction. Constant states remain consistent because physical Euler flux is linear in the normal vector. The construction also passes flux-reversal conservation and rotation tests.

This is a specified rotated-hybrid experiment, inspired by Nishikawa and Kitamura (2008). It is not the earlier pressure-sensor Roe/HLLE blend, and does not claim an optimized reproduction of the publication's Rotated-RHLL dissipation formula. The tiny-jump fallback and dimensional tolerance are explicit implementation choices.

What the forebody results establish#

The five fluxes are acoustically smoothed Roe, Einfeldt-type HLLE, AUSM+, AUSM+-up and directional HLLE/Roe. Each image shares one color range across its five field panels. The slip-wall pressure coefficient uses the actual wall-normal momentum flux; the two cells nearest the nose define the reported nose pressure.

The normal-shock jump followed by isentropic deceleration gives the inviscid centerline stagnation-pressure reference p0,2=46.8152057161. It is a scalar streamline reference, not an exact bow-shock field. The boundary layer and wake are absent. The nose pressure, reflection defect, remaining normalized update rate, positivity and integrated conservation residual are all saved.

On the fine seeded grid, Roe develops a large density reflection defect and its nose pressure falls to about 25.0. The fine HLLE nose pressure is about 47.38; the corresponding coarse value is about 48.81. The directional method and AUSM variants have different perturbation and grid responses. In particular, the directional method can amplify roundoff in its unperturbed control: a symmetric-looking initial state is not an exact discrete symmetry guarantee for that nonlinear direction selection. Inspect both controls and histories rather than selecting a single attractive image.

These are terminal snapshots of an evolving calculation. Nonzero update rates and two grid levels do not certify a converged steady solution, an asymptotic convergence order, or universal carbuncle freedom. Longer-time and time-step studies, other Mach numbers, rotated grids, external-code comparisons and further rotated-hybrid variants remain verification work. Full-cylinder viscous drag, lift, shedding and Strouhal validation are a separate task.

Reproduction and saved data#

Run MPLCONFIGDIR=.mplconfig python scripts/build_shock_expansion.py. The builder caches forebody runs only when the numerical source hashes and full configuration match. Download controls, diagnostics and source hashes and conserved states and mesh vertices/areas. Failed 1D entries include actual times and last accepted states; they must not be compared as if they reached the requested final time. All PNGs and the compressed arrays have hashes in the manifest.

The independent checks cover characteristic-domain integrals, switch selectivity, periodic conserved sums, pressure/velocity contact equilibrium, smooth refinement, AUSM branch identities and normal shocks, rotated-flux consistency/covariance, mesh closure and wall/global flux budgets. Passing these checks does not remove the flow-specific limits above.

Rotated Riemann sources: Ren (2003), Roe–Nishikawa et al. (2005), Nishikawa–Kitamura (2008) and the atlas experiment

site-coverage.title: Site coverage and counting rules
site-coverage.html:
Site coverage and counting rules

Published web edition, counted 2026-11-24. These are counts of catalog entries and documented examples, not a claim that every entry is a verified end-to-end solver.

94 equation/model entries · 163 methods and building blocks · 249 journal/conference papers · 310 total sources.

There are 9 saved-profile equation-gallery cases across 7 equation families, and 153 reading chapters including this inventory.

Equations and models#

Named equation/model entries, not scalar component equations or mathematically disjoint families. Includes frameworks and auxiliary formulations; variants share one entry except the three separately explained SR/GR fluid systems. Biological entries are imported once from their own catalog.

78 entries have scoped local examples; 16 are reading-only, including all 22 biological survey entries. A coupled system is one entry; its individual component equations do not increase the count. Poisson/Laplace and dimensional variants share entries. Named frameworks and specialized kinetic laws can both appear, so this is not a count of mathematically disjoint families.

Equation/model inventory#

Physics & mathematical models#

  • Linear advection — Local example.
  • Heat / diffusion — Local example.
  • Poisson / Laplace — Local example.
  • Inviscid Burgers — Local example.
  • LWR traffic flow — Local example.
  • Compressible Euler — Local example.
  • Shallow water, including the rotating linear model — Local example. Wet 1D flow and linear rotating Fourier symbols; no full geophysical dynamical core.
  • Isothermal Euler — Local example.
  • Ideal MHD — Local example.
  • Incompressible Navier–Stokes — Local example.
  • Isothermal lattice BGK — Local example.
  • Hamiltonian oscillators — Local example.
  • Gravitational particle model — Local example. Static force evaluations and boundary kernels; no coupled self-gravitating fluid evolution.
  • Bratu nonlinear boundary-value problem — Local example.
  • Auxiliary hyperbolic diffusion system — Local example. Periodic first-order steady-solution baseline, not physical-time heat diffusion.

Relativistic models#

  • Special-relativistic hydrodynamics — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver.
  • General-relativistic hydrodynamics — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver.
  • General-relativistic MHD — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver.
  • Relativistic radiation moments / M1 — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver.
  • Causal relativistic viscous fluid — Reading only. Literature review; no local relativistic solver.

Biological model survey#

  • Logistic population growth — Reading only. The linked original is the later 1847 memoir; the 1838 note itself was not audited. The differential equation is not the discrete logistic map.
  • Michaelis–Menten and full enzyme kinetics — Reading only. The 1913 rapid-equilibrium interpretation and the 1925 quasi-steady-state derivation must remain distinct.
  • Lotka–Volterra predator–prey — Reading only.
  • McKendrick age-structured population — Reading only. This is the classical age-transport form; the later von Foerster lineage is acknowledged without treating its date as the first appearance.
  • SIR and SEIR compartment models — Reading only. The original general epidemic framework is broader than this SIR specialization. Population-count and fraction conventions give different β definitions.
  • Fisher–KPP invasion front — Reading only. Fisher–KPP is a conventional family name; the independent KPP 1937 original remains an archival follow-up. The exact special speed is not the minimal speed.
  • Monod growth and chemostat — Reading only. This writes one constant-yield extension of saturation growth, not a universal metabolic model.
  • Hodgkin–Huxley membrane dynamics — Reading only. The original squid-axon model is not a calibrated human cardiac model. No single rate parameter set is selected by this survey.
  • Turing reaction–diffusion framework — Reading only. A spot image or unequal diffusion coefficients alone do not establish a Turing mechanism. Boundary conditions determine the available modes.
  • FitzHugh–Nagumo excitation and recovery — Reading only. This is a common normalized variant; cubic coefficients, recovery signs and nondimensionalization differ between formulations.
  • Keller–Segel chemotaxis — Reading only. This is a common two-field reduction of a more detailed original formulation. Blowup thresholds depend on dimension, domain, boundary and chemical dynamics.
  • Gierer–Meinhardt activator–inhibitor — Reading only. Source densities, saturation and baseline production vary across the model family. This simplified formula is not a verbatim transcription of every original variant.
  • Fluid–elastic structure and immersed boundaries — Reading only. Immersed boundary is a numerical coupling method, not itself a closed biological constitutive equation. The existing periodic MAC solver does not implement this coupling.
  • Chemical master equation and Gillespie SSA — Reading only. The 1977 paper is a foundational SSA reference, not a priority claim for all master equations. SSA is a solver; the reaction network is the model. A seed documents a trajectory, not an ensemble validation.
  • Mackey–Glass delayed physiological feedback — Reading only. A scalar initial value alone is insufficient. The delayed ODE is distinct from a spatial reaction–diffusion model.
  • Replicator evolutionary game dynamics — Reading only. No universal Lyapunov function or equivalence of fixed point and evolutionarily stable strategy is assumed.
  • Schnakenberg reaction–diffusion — Reading only. A mathematical chemical pattern model; matching a visual biological pattern does not calibrate it to a tissue.
  • Shigesada–Kawasaki–Teramoto cross-diffusion — Reading only. The displayed homogeneous-environment reduction omits the original environmental-potential terms. It is not equivalent to two independent scalar diffusion equations.
  • Gray–Scott spatial autocatalysis — Reading only. 1983 is the well-mixed CSTR source; Pearson 1993 is the spatial pattern reference. Spot division does not by itself demonstrate cell division or a linear Turing instability.
  • Aliev–Panfilov cardiac excitation — Reading only. Monodomain/bidomain tissue models add conductivity tensors and, for bidomain, an extracellular elliptic constraint. They are not automatically included by this two-variable model.
  • Repressilator mRNA–protein network — Reading only. The six-variable form is distinct from a reduced three-protein oscillator; oscillations are parameter-dependent.
  • Genetic toggle switch — Reading only. Bistability is not guaranteed for arbitrary Hill exponents or production rates. Induction, mRNA dynamics and noise are additional model choices.

Numerical method inventory#

Named numerical methods and building blocks with a reading chapter. Aliases count once; RK stages, dimensions, parameter combinations, mesh layouts and theoretical conditions do not add methods. A family and a separately explained algorithm may both appear. Not a count of mutually exclusive end-to-end solvers.

153 entries have scoped local examples; 10 are reading-only. Reconstruction limiters, preconditioners and coupling operators are building blocks, not complete PDE solvers. Mesh layouts, CFL conditions and theorems are not counted as numerical methods.

Spatial discretization#

  • Euler characteristic reconstruction — Local example. Local conservative FV basis or face-frozen Roe FD basis; controlled component/characteristic comparisons.
  • FD WENO5-Z — Local example. Global LF splitting, exponent 2, fixed epsilon 1e-6; point values, not FV state interpolation.

Riemann fluxes & corrections#

  • HLLD MHD Riemann solver — Local example. Full-vector adiabatic HLLD/HLLE with Brio-Wu, circular Alfven refinement and weak field-loop tests. CT-Contact and GLM, not UCT-HLLD.
  • AUSM-family flux splitting — Local example. Arithmetic-sound-speed AUSM plus specified critical-sound-speed AUSM+ and AUSM+-up. Matched traced-PPM cases, a recorded strong-jump failure and forebody tests; no low-Mach PDE certification.

Limiters & admissibility#

Time integration#

Linear & nonlinear solvers#

Coupling, constraints & particles#

  • GLM divergence cleaning — Local example. Original Rusanov OT baseline plus HLLD/HLLE loop tests with an exact longitudinal cleaning solve and split damping. Native cell-centered divergence.

Particle fields & gravity#

Additional formulations#

Element bases & approximation#

  • Legendre modal basis / orthonormal scaling — Local example. Reference-element tabulation, derivatives, projection and affine mass/stiffness matrices.
  • Lagrange nodal basis / GLL collocation — Local example. Interval cardinal functions, modal transforms, exact versus quadrature mass, and P1/P2 triangle shapes.

Papers versus all sources#

Unique bibliographic publications classified as journal articles or conference papers, deduplicated by DOI or author/title/year. Includes reviews, translations and explicitly labeled accepted papers; not a claim that every full text was inspected. Books, chapters, reports, preprints and documentation are separate.

Unique cataloged works across all publication types. An original publication and a later translation are separate works; duplicate DOI records are not. NASA case links in prose are not catalog records.

A duplicate Cockburn–Shu 1989 record was merged. Burgers 1948 is classified as a book chapter. The former 146-record total included that duplicate; subsequent source additions are reflected in the current unique-work totals above. An original paper and a separately published translation remain separate works. The bibliography does not claim that every full text has been inspected; source notes preserve the inspection status.

Reproduction#

The named registry is catalog/coverage.json; biological entries and publication types come from their respective catalogs. python scripts/build_coverage.py checks unique publication identities and local reading links, then generates the counts and this inventory. The website build runs that audit before rendering. Parameter choices, time frames, repeated equations in prose and test function counts do not increase these totals.

sparse-nonlinear.title: Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual
sparse-nonlinear.html:
Sparse and nonlinear systems: measure the actual residual

Implemented: COO-to-CSR assembly, restarted GMRES, BiCGSTAB, Jacobi and unpivoted ILU(0), and Armijo-damped Newton with dense or Krylov inner solves. These are small, inspectable real-arithmetic examples.

1986–1992: nonsymmetric Krylov methods#

Saad–Schultz (1986) introduces GMRES; van der Vorst (1992) introduces BiCGSTAB. The implemented GMRES uses Arnoldi reorthogonalization and small Hessenberg least squares, restarting after a specified number of inner iterations. BiCGSTAB has explicit breakdown reporting; it need not have monotone residuals.

Both implementations apply a fixed right preconditioner:

AM−1z=b,x=M−1z,∥b−Ax∥2≤max⁡(atol,rtol∥b∥2). A M^{-1} z=b,\qquad x=M^{-1}z, \qquad \|b-Ax\|_2\leq\max(\mathrm{atol},\mathrm{rtol}\|b\|_2). AM−1z=b,x=M−1z,∥b−Ax∥2​≤max(atol,rtol∥b∥2​).

The stopping history recomputes the true residual. Jacobi uses diagonal scaling. ILU(0) retains the supplied nonzero structure, with no fill, pivoting or reordering; tiny pivots raise an explicit failure. This is not a robust replacement for a production sparse factorization.

Newton and conditioning#

Newton solves J(x)δ=−F(x), then chooses a backtracked step length with an Armijo residual decrease. The Newton–Krylov demonstration assembles J and uses GMRES; it is not matrix free. Bratu's equation is checked against an analytic solution at two spatial resolutions, including inner-solve failures.

A small residual is not automatically a small solution error:

∥x−x^∥∥x∥≤κ(A)∥b−Ax^∥∥b∥. \frac{\|x-\hat x\|}{\|x\|} \leq \kappa(A)\frac{\|b-A\hat x\|}{\|b\|}. ∥x∥∥x−x^∥​≤κ(A)∥b∥∥b−Ax^∥​.

Condition number, eigenvalue distribution and nonnormality describe different features. A smaller condition number alone does not rank restarted GMRES. CG still requires an SPD operator and suitable SPD preconditioning; generic ILU(0) is not asserted to satisfy that requirement.

The nonsymmetric example is first-order upwind advection plus centered diffusion with zero Dirichlet data. Iteration counts have different per-iteration costs; the figure makes no wall-clock ranking. See the data and source hashes, FEM assembly, and implicit ODE stages.

Shared foundation: automatic differentiation and Bratu verification

Compare analytic, finite-difference and forward-mode AD with the same residual, initial state and Newton stopping controls. Derivative error, nonlinear residual and spatial discretization error are reported separately, with dedicated code, eight tests and reproduction commands. A separate Bratu parameter-sensitivity chapter verifies implicit differentiation and discrete adjoints. A reverse-mode AD engine remains unimplemented.

stability.title: Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax
stability.html:
Differences, CFL, von Neumann analysis, and Lax

Try the interactive stability laboratory and read the experiment guide to connect the formulas below with live browser calculations.

Choose space and time discretizations separately#

Forward, backward, and centered spatial differences are

D+uj=uj+1−ujh,D−uj=uj−uj−1h,D0uj=uj+1−uj−12h. D_+u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_j}{h},\qquad D_-u_j=\frac{u_j-u_{j-1}}h,\qquad D_0u_j=\frac{u_{j+1}-u_{j-1}}{2h}. D+​uj​=huj+1​−uj​​,D−​uj​=huj​−uj−1​​,D0​uj​=2huj+1​−uj−1​​.

For smooth functions, the first two are first-order accurate and the centered stencil is second order. Compare them with numart.advection.finite_difference. For linear advection u_t+a u_x=0, upwinding follows information propagation: use a backward difference for a>0 and a forward difference for a<0. A forward difference is therefore not synonymous with an upwind difference.

Forward Euler in time gives u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^n; backward Euler gives u^{n+1}=u^n+Δt L_h u^{n+1} and requires a system solve. A backward spatial stencil alone does not make a method implicit.

CFL: can the stencil reach the information it needs?#

For constant-coefficient periodic advection with an explicit nearest-neighbor stencil, domain-of-dependence reasoning requires |a|Δt/h ≤ 1. The constant changes with the stencil, Runge–Kutta method, DG degree, and dimension. Explicit diffusion introduces a Δt=O(h²) restriction. A CFL condition is generally necessary rather than sufficient for stability. Courant–Friedrichs–Lewy (1928).

Forward-time, centered-space (FTCS) advection is a counterexample. Substituting a Fourier mode u_j^n=G^n e^{ijθ} gives

G=1−iCsin⁡θ,∣G∣2=1+C2sin⁡2θ,C=aΔt/h. G=1-i C\sin θ,\quad |G|^2=1+C^2\sin^2 θ, \qquad C=a\Delta t/h. G=1−iCsinθ,∣G∣2=1+C2sin2θ,C=aΔt/h.

Some modes grow even when |C|<1. The scheme is unstable under ordinary fixed-CFL grid refinement.

Lax–Friedrichs and Lax–Wendroff#

The classical Lax–Friedrichs scheme is

ujn+1=12(uj+1n+uj−1n)−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n),G=cos⁡θ−iCsin⁡θ. u_j^{n+1}=\tfrac12(u_{j+1}^n+u_{j-1}^n) -\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n),\qquad G=\cos θ-iC\sin θ. ujn+1​=21​(uj+1n​+uj−1n​)−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​),G=cosθ−iCsinθ.

Since |G|²=1-(1-C²)sin²θ, periodic linear advection is stable for |C|≤1. Classical LF uses the numerical-viscosity coefficient h/Δt. Rusanov uses a local maximum wave speed; WENO here uses global LF flux splitting. These are different discrete constructions. Lax (1954).

Lax–Wendroff is

ujn+1=ujn−C2(uj+1n−uj−1n)+C22(uj+1n−2ujn+uj−1n), u_j^{n+1}=u_j^n-\tfrac C2(u_{j+1}^n-u_{j-1}^n) +\tfrac{C^2}{2}(u_{j+1}^n-2u_j^n+u_{j-1}^n), ujn+1​=ujn​−2C​(uj+1n​−uj−1n​)+2C2​(uj+1n​−2ujn​+uj−1n​),
G=1−iCsin⁡θ+C2(cos⁡θ−1),∣G∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin⁡4(θ/2). G=1-iC\sin θ+C^2(\cos θ-1),\quad |G|^2=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4(θ/2). G=1−iCsinθ+C2(cosθ−1),∣G∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin4(θ/2).

Its stability condition for this problem is also |C|≤1. Second-order accuracy does not itself suppress oscillations near discontinuities. Lax–Wendroff (1960).

Tests compare the analytical amplification factors from amplification with actual mode evolution from difference_step. The gallery seeds a small Nyquist perturbation and compares C=0.8 with C=1.1.

Dissipation and dispersion: read amplitude and phase separately#

The same amplification factor used to test growth also explains two distinct errors: numerical dissipation damps a wave's amplitude; numerical dispersion changes its propagation speed in a wavelength-dependent way. Consider constant-speed scalar advection on a periodic uniform grid. Let h be the grid spacing, Δt the positive time step, k the wavenumber, θ the dimensionless grid wavenumber, and C the signed Courant number. The Fourier convention and exact one-step factor are

ut+aux=0,xj=jh,θ=kh,C=aΔth,ujn=u^ neijθ,Gexact=e−iakΔt=e−iCθ.\begin{gathered}u_t+a u_x=0,\qquad x_j=jh,\quad\theta=kh,\quad C=\frac{a\Delta t}{h},\\u_j^n=\widehat u^{\,n}e^{ij\theta},\qquad G_{\rm exact}=e^{-ia k\Delta t}=e^{-iC\theta}.\end{gathered}ut​+aux​=0,xj​=jh,θ=kh,C=haΔt​,ujn​=uneijθ,Gexact​=e−iakΔt=e−iCθ.​

The exact solution translates without changing amplitude. This makes the model useful for separating artificial damping from transport error.

Compare dissipation and dispersion through wave evolution

Compare the same smooth initial pulse at the same times and on identical axes. Dashed black is exact advection; solid color is the panel result. A isolates upwind damping as a constructed diagnostic, B evolves the centered semidiscrete equation exactly in time, and C is Lax–Wendroff.

Loading the wave data. The static comparison below remains available without playback.

Here, “no dissipation preserves amplitude” means preserving the magnitude of each Fourier component. When their phases separate, the combined peak can change height and the profile can develop negative tails or oscillations. Watch B change shape while its discrete L2 ratio stays at one. A lower peak alone is not proof of dissipation.

View matched-time static snapshots
Conditions, formulas and reproduction files

The periodic domain is [0,1), with a=1, N=127 and C=0.8, so Δt=0.8/127. One circuit takes T=L/a=1. The player shows every second step from 0 to 160 (about 1.008 circuits). The initial periodic pulse is

u(x,0)=exp⁡ ⁣[60(cos⁡ ⁣(2π(x−14))−1)].u(x,0)=\exp\!\left[60\left(\cos\!\left(2\pi(x-\tfrac14)\right)-1\right)\right].u(x,0)=exp[60(cos(2π(x−41​))−1)].

For θ=2πm/N, the one-step multipliers underlying the saved frames are below. A is not actual upwind evolution: its phase error is removed to isolate damping. No RK4 or other time discretization is added to B.

GA=∣1−C+Ce−iθ∣e−iCθ,GB=e−iCsin⁡θ,GC=1−iCsin⁡θ+C2(cos⁡θ−1).\begin{aligned}G_A&=\left|1-C+Ce^{-i\theta}\right|e^{-iC\theta},\\G_B&=e^{-iC\sin\theta},\\G_C&=1-iC\sin\theta+C^2(\cos\theta-1).\end{aligned}GA​GB​GC​​=​1−C+Ce−iθ​e−iCθ,=e−iCsinθ,=1−iCsinθ+C2(cosθ−1).​

Curves are computed from the trigonometric interpolant of the initial samples. The dashed reference was checked against analytic pulse translation at every saved step and grid point, with maximum error about 1.3×10⁻¹⁴ under these conditions. C was independently checked against real-space Lax–Wendroff updates. Display JSON is rounded to seven decimal places, with error at most 5×10⁻⁸.

All frames JSON · Selected snapshots CSV · Conditions and results JSON · Checks and hashes JSON · Generator Python · Requirements · Run instructions · Script license

Save the generator and requirements in one folder, then run with a new output directory. Figures, data and prose retain the site’s item-specific reuse terms.

python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python generate-wave-evolution.py --output generated

What the amplification factor measures#

For a linear, translation-invariant one-step scheme, write its factor in polar form:

G(θ)=∣G(θ)∣e−iϕ(θ),u^ n=G(θ)nu^ 0,∣u^ n∣∣u^ 0∣=∣G(θ)∣n.\begin{aligned}G(\theta)&=|G(\theta)|e^{-i\phi(\theta)},\\\widehat u^{\,n}&=G(\theta)^n\widehat u^{\,0},\qquad\frac{|\widehat u^{\,n}|}{|\widehat u^{\,0}|}=|G(\theta)|^n.\end{aligned}G(θ)un​=∣G(θ)∣e−iϕ(θ),=G(θ)nu0,∣u0∣∣un∣​=∣G(θ)∣n.​

Thus |G|<1 damps this mode; repeated steps accumulate the loss. |G|=1 preserves its amplitude, while |G|>1 amplifies it. For this scalar periodic problem, the familiar requirement |G|≤1 controls growth, but says nothing about whether the amplitude stays close to its exact value of one.

For 0<|G|, the loss can also be expressed as a damping rate σnum per unit time:

σnum=−log⁡∣G∣Δt,∣u^ n∣=e−σnumtn∣u^ 0∣,tn=nΔt.\begin{aligned}\sigma_{\rm num}&=-\frac{\log|G|}{\Delta t},\\|\widehat u^{\,n}|&=e^{-\sigma_{\rm num}t_n}|\widehat u^{\,0}|,\qquad t_n=n\Delta t.\end{aligned}σnum​∣un∣​=−Δtlog∣G∣​,=e−σnum​tn​∣u0∣,tn​=nΔt.​

This is a decay rate with units of inverse time, not a diffusion coefficient. At G=0 the mode vanishes in one step; a finite damping rate and phase are undefined.

Phase needs a sign convention as well. Use arg₀ for an argument continued from G(0)=1 along a branch on which G never vanishes. The minus sign matches the exact factor above:

ϕ(θ)=−arg⁡0G(θ),ωnum=ϕ(θ)Δt,cnuma=ωnum/ka=ϕ(θ)Cθ(ak≠0).\begin{aligned}\phi(\theta)&=-\arg_0G(\theta),\qquad\omega_{\rm num}=\frac{\phi(\theta)}{\Delta t},\\\frac{c_{\rm num}}a&=\frac{\omega_{\rm num}/k}a=\frac{\phi(\theta)}{C\theta}\qquad(ak\ne0).\end{aligned}ϕ(θ)acnum​​​=−arg0​G(θ),ωnum​=Δtϕ(θ)​,=aωnum​/k​=Cθϕ(θ)​(ak=0).​

Correct transport requires φ=Cθ, as well as |G|=1. A stable wave can travel at the wrong speed and accumulate a large position error. At θ=0, use the low-wavenumber limit for the speed ratio. At G=0 the scheme has removed the mode and its phase is undefined. Principal arguments wrap by 2π; treating that jump as a physical change gives a false dispersion curve. At the Nyquist endpoints θ=±π, the sampled modes coincide, so their propagation direction cannot be uniquely recovered from grid samples.

Three examples reveal different errors#

For a>0, forward Euler with backward spatial differencing is the first-order upwind scheme. Direct substitution gives

Gup=1−C(1−e−iθ),∣Gup∣2=1−4C(1−C)sin⁡2 ⁣(θ2),0≤C≤1(a>0).\begin{aligned}G_{\rm up}&=1-C(1-e^{-i\theta}),\\|G_{\rm up}|^2&=1-4C(1-C)\sin^2\!\left(\frac\theta2\right),\\&\hspace{1em}0\le C\le1\qquad(a>0).\end{aligned}Gup​∣Gup​∣2​=1−C(1−e−iθ),=1−4C(1−C)sin2(2θ​),0≤C≤1(a>0).​

For 0<C<1, every nonconstant resolved Fourier mode is damped. This is numerical dissipation: the underlying advection equation has no physical decay. Its phase generally also differs from Cθ. For a<0, reverse the upwind stencil.

Centered differencing with time still continuous instead gives

dujdt=−auj+1−uj−12h,λh=−iahsin⁡θ,ωh=ahsin⁡θ,cha=sin⁡θθ.\begin{aligned}\frac{d u_j}{dt}&=-a\frac{u_{j+1}-u_{j-1}}{2h},\qquad\lambda_h=-i\frac ah\sin\theta,\\\omega_h&=\frac ah\sin\theta,\qquad\frac{c_h}a=\frac{\sin\theta}{\theta}.\end{aligned}dtduj​​ωh​​=−a2huj+1​−uj−1​​,λh​=−iha​sinθ,=ha​sinθ,ach​​=θsinθ​.​

The eigenvalue is purely imaginary, so this semidiscrete mode has no amplitude decay. Yet sinθ/θ differs from one: it is dispersive. For θ=π/2, the phase speed is only 2/π≈0.637 times a. At θ=π the centered derivative vanishes, a stationary Nyquist checkerboard annihilated by the centered derivative, rather than correct transport.

Time discretization changes the result. With forward Euler,

GFE+centered=1−iCsin⁡θ,∣GFE+centered∣2=1+C2sin⁡2θ.\begin{aligned}G_{\rm FE+centered}&=1-iC\sin\theta,\\|G_{\rm FE+centered}|^2&=1+C^2\sin^2\theta.\end{aligned}GFE+centered​∣GFE+centered​∣2​=1−iCsinθ,=1+C2sin2θ.​

Modes with sinθ≠0 grow for any nonzero C, explaining the FTCS instability discussed above. Other time integrators have different amplitude and phase responses on the same spatial eigenvalues. The linearized centered-wave discussion in KEEP and its RK4 amplitude and phase analysis make this separation explicit.

For Lax–Wendroff (1960), the factor already derived above also yields

GLW=1−iCsin⁡θ+C2(cos⁡θ−1),∣GLW∣2=1−4C2(1−C2)sin⁡4 ⁣(θ2).\begin{aligned}G_{\rm LW}&=1-iC\sin\theta+C^2(\cos\theta-1),\\|G_{\rm LW}|^2&=1-4C^2(1-C^2)\sin^4\!\left(\frac\theta2\right).\end{aligned}GLW​∣GLW​∣2​=1−iCsinθ+C2(cosθ−1),=1−4C2(1−C2)sin4(2θ​).​

At generic 0<|C|<1 it therefore has amplitude error as well as phase error; calling it “purely dispersive” is incorrect. Its leading smooth-wave error can be dispersive without eliminating higher-order damping. At C=1, both upwind and Lax–Wendroff reduce to G=e−iθ, an exact one-cell shift on this grid. This special Courant number is not representative of other step sizes.

For C=0.8 and θ=π/2 (four grid spacings per wavelength), the one-step amplitude gain is about 0.8246 for upwind and 0.8773 for Lax–Wendroff. Their phase-speed ratios are about 1.0551 and 0.9135, respectively: the first travels too fast and the second too slowly. Both are stable, yet both have amplitude and phase errors.

Keep the physical and numerical questions distinct#

If the physical PDE includes viscosity or another decay mechanism, the exact |G| can itself be below one for the mode considered; compare numerical damping with that exact decay. Likewise, a physically dispersive PDE has a wavenumber-dependent exact phase speed. Error means disagreement with the physical reference.

A-stability and L-stability classify a time integrator's response to linear test modes; neither guarantees accurate wave propagation at a chosen resolution. The formulas here concern scalar periodic linear advection. They do not certify nonlinear Euler dynamics, shocks, or wall boundary treatments.

A useful diagnostic first fixes h and reduces Δt to expose the time integrator's contribution. Then reduce h with temporal error controlled. Refining with C held fixed changes both scales and does not by itself separate the two errors. For a smooth single mode, compare amplitude and unwrapped phase at the same physical time; agreement in only one of these quantities is incomplete evidence of accuracy.

The formulas and worked values here follow by directly substituting Fourier modes into the displayed differences. For the assumptions of the analysis and comparison against the exact amplification factor, see R. R. Rosales’s author lecture notes (2022), §1 and §1.1.2.

The Lax–Richtmyer equivalence theorem#

Consider a well-posed linear initial-value problem in an appropriate Banach space and a consistent linear difference approximation. When stability means uniform boundedness of the discrete evolution operators over a fixed finite time interval, stability is equivalent to convergence. Lax–Richtmyer (1956), original paper.

Writing the error as e^{n+1}=S_h e^n+Δt τ^n, the bound ||S_h^m||≤M_T gives ||e^n||≤M_T||e^0||+M_T T max||τ^k||. Consistency makes the truncation-error term tend to zero, providing the basic stability-to-convergence argument. The converse requires a uniform-boundedness argument.

The theorem does not directly certify nonlinear Euler, WENO, shocks, or arbitrary boundary treatments. The Fourier criterion |G|≤1 used here applies to periodic, constant-coefficient scalar problems. Boundaries, variable coefficients, nonnormal matrices, and multistep schemes need additional analysis.

Time steps in the first edition#

  • Euler and barotropic systems: Δt=C h/max(|u|+c), with default C=0.3.
  • DG: Δt=C h/((2p+1)|a|), with default C=0.2.
  • 2D MHD: Δt=C/[max(s_x)/h+max(s_y)/h], with default C=0.3.

These conservative choices are checked on selected examples. They are not rigorous nonlinear stability limits for every initial condition.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

stiff-integration.title: Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error
stiff-integration.html:
Stiff integration: solve the stage, control the time error

Implemented: backward Euler, constant-step BDF2 with backward-Euler startup, two-stage SDIRK2, first-order IMEX Euler, and adaptive SDIRK2 by step doubling. All nonlinear stages use damped Newton and report failure explicitly.

Implicit stages and stability#

Backward Euler solves y_new−y_old−h f(t_new,y_new)=0. BDF2 solves

3yn+1−4yn+yn−12h=f(tn+1,yn+1). \frac{3y_{n+1}-4y_n+y_{n-1}}{2h}=f(t_{n+1},y_{n+1}). 2h3yn+1​−4yn​+yn−1​​=f(tn+1​,yn+1​).

Alexander (1977) is the source for the L-stable, two-stage, second-order singly diagonally implicit family used here:

γ=1−1/2,A=(γ01−γγ),b=(1−γ,γ),c=(γ,1). \gamma=1-1/\sqrt2,\qquad A=\begin{pmatrix}\gamma&0\\1-\gamma&\gamma\end{pmatrix}, \quad b=(1-\gamma,\gamma),\quad c=(\gamma,1). γ=1−1/2​,A=(γ1−γ​0γ​),b=(1−γ,γ),c=(γ,1).

Each diagonal stage is a separate nonlinear solve. An implicit method can permit steps beyond an explicit stability limit, while accuracy still limits useful step size. A converged Newton residual measures the stage equation, not the temporal discretization error.

Adaptive and split steps#

The adaptive implementation compares one full SDIRK2 step with two half steps. The local error estimate is (y_half−y_full)/3, scaled by atol+rtol max(|y_old|,|y_half|). It accepts the two-half-step value, without Richardson extrapolation, and adjusts h with exponent −1/3. Rejected trials and accepted steps are counted; reaching a trial limit raises an error.

IMEX Euler evaluates one part explicitly and the other implicitly. This minimal first-order split is not the higher-order IMEX RK constructions of Ascher–Ruuth–Spiteri (1997). The explicit part retains its own stability restriction. Variable-step BDF, embedded DIRK pairs and operator splitting remain extensions.

The stiff test y′=−1000(y−cos t)−sin t has exact solution cos t when y(0)=1. The manifest records maximum errors at actual integration nodes and adaptive step counts. Separate tests verify order on a nonlinear, nonautonomous ODE and strong damping of a stiff decay mode.

The coarse stiff-forced refinement is not in a uniform second-order regime. BDF2 startup and stiff order reduction affect the maximum-over-nodes error; the nonlinear nonstiff order test checks the formal temporal order separately.

For definitions and comparisons of A-stability, L-stability and L1/L2/L∞ error norms, see the shared accuracy and stability guide.

symplectic.title: Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise
symplectic.html:
Symplectic integration: a canonical map, not an exact energy promise

A symplectic integrator advances a Hamiltonian system while preserving its canonical two-form. This is the map property behind the good long-time behavior of many orbital and particle integrators. It does not generally preserve the original Hamiltonian exactly. The Hamiltonian map notebook separates those two questions with computed examples.

What the map preserves#

For state z = (q,p), Hamilton’s equations and the symplectic condition are

z˙=J∇H(z),J=(0I−I0),DΦh(z)TJDΦh(z)=J. \dot z=J\nabla H(z),\qquad J=\begin{pmatrix}0&I\\-I&0\end{pmatrix}, \qquad D\Phi_h(z)^T J D\Phi_h(z)=J. z˙=J∇H(z),J=(0−I​I0​),DΦh​(z)TJDΦh​(z)=J.

The last identity says that each numerical step is a canonical transformation. For one degree of freedom it is equivalent to det(D Phi) = 1, preserving oriented phase-plane area. In higher dimensions, preservation of total volume alone is weaker than symplecticity.

Three separate properties should be tested: preservation of the two-form, preservation of H, and time symmetry Phi_(−h) = Phi_h^(−1). Symplectic Euler already illustrates the distinction: it is symplectic but is neither exactly energy preserving nor time symmetric in general.

Split the Hamiltonian, compose exact subflows#

For a unit-mass separable system H(q,p) = p²/2 + V(q), the two subflows are a drift and a kick:

Dh(q,p)=(q+hp,p),Kh(q,p)=(q,p−h∇V(q)). D_h(q,p)=(q+hp,p),\qquad K_h(q,p)=(q,p-h\nabla V(q)). Dh​(q,p)=(q+hp,p),Kh​(q,p)=(q,p−h∇V(q)).

Each is symplectic; compositions remain symplectic. The notebook includes kick–drift symplectic Euler, and the symmetric second-order Störmer–Verlet update

pn+1/2=pn−h2∇V(qn),qn+1=qn+hpn+1/2,pn+1=pn+1/2−h2∇V(qn+1). p_{n+1/2}=p_n-\frac h2\nabla V(q_n),\quad q_{n+1}=q_n+h p_{n+1/2},\quad p_{n+1}=p_{n+1/2}-\frac h2\nabla V(q_{n+1}). pn+1/2​=pn​−2h​∇V(qn​),qn+1​=qn​+hpn+1/2​,pn+1​=pn+1/2​−2h​∇V(qn+1​).

This is the mechanical Leapfrog/velocity-Verlet formulation. It differs from the two-step scalar recurrence in the earlier time-integration notebook.

Fourth order by composition#

Writing S2(h) for a Verlet step, one fourth-order composition is

S4(h)=S2(ah) S2(bh) S2(ah),a=12−21/3,b=−21/32−21/3. S_4(h)=S_2(a h)\,S_2(b h)\,S_2(a h),\qquad a=\frac1{2-2^{1/3}},\quad b=-\frac{2^{1/3}}{2-2^{1/3}}. S4​(h)=S2​(ah)S2​(bh)S2​(ah),a=2−21/31​,b=−2−21/321/3​.

Yoshida (1990) develops higher-order symplectic compositions. Here b is negative: an internal substep goes backward in time. The construction is suitable for the smooth conservative examples used here; simply applying it to irreversible diffusion, shocks, or collision handling is not justified. Higher order also does not establish unconditional stability or an equal-cost advantage.

Energy and a modified Hamiltonian#

Backward error analysis describes a nearby, generally formal modified Hamiltonian. Under smoothness, bounded-trajectory, small-step, and related hypotheses, this explains small long-time energy errors. It does not assert an exact invariant of the original H for every orbit or step size. Hairer, Lubich, and Wanner (2003) develop this geometric viewpoint and its assumptions.

For the special oscillator H = (p²+q²)/2, kick–drift–kick Verlet preserves the quadratic invariant

Ih=12p2+12(1−h24)q2 I_h=\frac12p^2+\frac12\left(1-\frac{h^2}{4}\right)q^2 Ih​=21​p2+21​(1−4h2​)q2

up to roundoff. H itself oscillates. This invariant is not a claim that its unscaled Hamiltonian flow is exactly the numerical time-h map. The oscillator map is bounded for |h| < 2; above that limit it can be symplectic and unstable.

Implicit midpoint and RK4 as comparisons#

Implicit midpoint is symplectic and time symmetric when its endpoint equation is solved accurately. It preserves the quadratic oscillator H to roundoff here. It need not exactly conserve a nonquadratic H. Classical RK4 is fourth order but is generally neither symplectic nor time symmetric. Good short-time accuracy alone does not certify the map’s geometry.

The second test problem is H = p²/2 + q²/2 + q⁴/4, a smooth nonlinear oscillator. It makes midpoint’s special quadratic-energy conservation visibly distinguishable from a general claim.

Reproducible notebook and checks#

from numart.hamiltonian import trajectory, energy, canonical_step, J
t, z = trajectory(h=0.2, steps=1000, method='yoshida4', system='quartic')
print(max(abs((energy(z, 'quartic')-energy(z[0], 'quartic'))/energy(z[0], 'quartic'))))
_, M = canonical_step([0.7, 0.4], 0.2, 'yoshida4', 'quartic', True)
print(M.T @ J @ M - J)

The computed dataset and source manifest supplies 30 Python trajectories: five methods, two Hamiltonians, and h = 0.1, 0.2, or 0.4, all to T = 200 from (q,p) = (1,0.2). Plotted trajectories contain at most 1001 samples; maximum energy errors use every integration step. The phase-patch view applies one step to a square centered at (0.7,0.4). Its sampled polygon boundary is an illustration; the displayed local defect uses an analytic map Jacobian at the patch center.

Tests check refinement orders against the exact oscillator, analytic Jacobians against independent finite differences, the canonical identity on both potentials, time reversal for symmetric methods, the Verlet quadratic invariant, and the difference between quadratic and nonquadratic midpoint energy. The gallery and notebook are educational fixed-step examples, not orbit-accuracy or timing rankings.

Connecting to particle gravity#

A fixed step and a force that is the gradient of a consistent position-dependent potential support the splitting argument. A generic approximate Tree force, changing opening decisions, ad hoc mesh interpolation, or state-dependent step selection does not automatically retain that proof. Force approximation and time integration need joint tests. Continue with particle gravity and Poisson solvers and gravity boundary kernels.

textbooks.title: Textbooks: where to look next
textbooks.html:
Textbooks: where to look next

A working bookshelf for this atlas. Choose a book by the question you need to answer; this is a reading guide, not a ranking. Bibliographic years below identify the cited editions, not the invention dates of algorithms.

The links lead to publisher records or author-maintained pages. We checked edition metadata and available descriptions or contents, not every derivation in every book. Chapter suggestions describe the atlas connection; they do not claim that all of a textbook has been implemented.

A short starting path: Hirsch for the CFD framework; LeVeque for conservation laws and finite-volume reasoning; Toro for Riemann solvers; Patankar for pressure–velocity coupling; Saad for sparse iterative solves. Return to original papers when tracing a particular algorithm.

time-integration.title: Time integration and leapfrog
time-integration.html:
Time integration and leapfrog

Spatial reconstruction and time integration are independent choices. After spatial discretization, a PDE becomes an ODE system dU/dt = L(U). Accuracy, stability, monotonicity, dissipation, and cost then depend on both parts. The time integration notebook isolates the temporal choice using y′ = i y, y(0) = 1.

Twelve methods on one oscillator#

The exact solution exp(i t) follows the unit circle. Forward Euler and backward Euler are first order: the former grows on this undamped oscillator, while the latter damps it. The explicit RK2 family includes Heun / SSPRK(2,2), explicit midpoint, and Ralston. Kutta RK3, SSPRK(3,3), and SSPRK(4,3) are third order; classical RK4 and SSPRK(5,4) are fourth order. Implicit midpoint is second order and preserves the amplitude of this linear oscillator. Its phase still has error. Read the RK family chapter and use the family notebook for stage/order/SSP comparisons and nonlinear tests.

For y′ = lambda y, define z = lambda delta t. One-step amplification factors include

RFE=1+z,RBE=11−z,Rmidpoint=1+z/21−z/2. R_{\rm FE}=1+z,\quad R_{\rm BE}=\frac1{1-z},\quad R_{\rm midpoint}=\frac{1+z/2}{1-z/2}. RFE​=1+z,RBE​=1−z1​,Rmidpoint​=1−z/21+z/2​.

The RK factors are the exponential Taylor polynomial through degree two, three, or four for the three RK2 variants, Kutta RK3 / SSPRK(3,3), or classical RK4 on this scalar linear equation. SSPRK(4,3) instead has a degree-four term z⁴/48; SSPRK(5,4) has an additional degree-five term. Shared scalar amplification does not make nonlinear RK stages identical. SSP properties depend on a forward-Euler bound for the spatial operator; they are not unconditional stability.

Leapfrog needs two roots#

The centered, two-step first-order-system recurrence is

yn+1=yn−1+2zyn,ξ±=z±1+z2. y^{n+1}=y^{n-1}+2z y^n,\qquad \xi_\pm=z\pm\sqrt{1+z^2}. yn+1=yn−1+2zyn,ξ±​=z±1+z2​.

The root tending to +1 as z tends to zero carries the physical mode; the root tending to −1 carries a computational mode alternating between steps. Both roots and their multiplicities matter. For z = i sigma, distinct roots have unit modulus when |sigma| < 1. At |sigma| = 1 the repeated root can give linearly growing solutions; do not include that endpoint in a general boundedness claim. Above it, one root grows geometrically.

A starting value is required in addition to y(0). This implementation takes one RK4 step, optionally adding a real perturbation epsilon to y(1). At lambda = 0 that perturbation gives even samples equal to 1 and odd samples equal to 1+epsilon: a direct computational-mode demonstration. For the notebook’s oscillator it also perturbs the physical mode.

Time filters such as the Robert–Asselin family modify this behavior, with their own damping and accuracy tradeoffs; see Williams (2009). No filter is applied in this edition.

Particle leapfrog is a different formulation#

A staggered kick–drift scheme for position and velocity, or velocity Verlet for a second-order mechanical system, is often also called leapfrog. Its variables live at different temporal locations and its symplectic interpretation uses that structure. The scalar recurrence above is not a demonstration of a complete SPH particle integrator or a proof of long-time energy conservation for general mechanics.

Reproduce and read the notebook#

from numart.time_integration import linear_trajectory, leapfrog_roots
t, y = linear_trajectory(rate=1j, dt=0.1, steps=200, method='leapfrog')
print(leapfrog_roots(0.1j))

The browser selects from Python-computed trajectories with fixed final time 20, twelve methods, seven step sizes, and three leapfrog starting perturbations. Axes expand for unstable samples. A matching time interval is not an equal-cost comparison: implicit solves and RK stages differ. Tests measure temporal refinement orders and check the leapfrog roots, alternating mode, and midpoint amplitude. These oscillator trajectories evaluate the scalar stability factor, which is algebraically equivalent to RK stages on this linear test equation; the separate family notebook evaluates full nonlinear stages.

Continue with the spatial stability laboratory, SPH, and ALE.

Canonical mechanical maps#

The symplectic integration chapter now implements mechanical kick–drift–kick Verlet, a fourth-order Yoshida composition, symplectic Euler, and implicit midpoint on harmonic and quartic Hamiltonians. The map notebook compares them with RK4, separating canonical structure from exact energy conservation.

An operator-splitting reading now compares first-order Lie–Trotter and second-order Strang with a small exact-flow illustration. It does not add a general splitting implementation to this chapter’s existing solver package. A lightweight fixed-input example now runs both on the same reaction–diffusion problem.

quantum-chemistry.title: Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations
quantum-chemistry.html:
ELECTRONIC STRUCTURE · QUANTUM CHEMISTRY · DFT

Quantum chemistry and DFT: approximations and equations

From Schrödinger, HF and DFT to bases, SCF and correlation, including space groups, little-group irreps, SOC and time reversal in band calculations.

Bilingual reading for 20 entries and 36 primary publications. Runnable validation covers two hydrogenic/He families and scoped finite-basis H₂ RHF. A fixed periodic-He LDA workflow is also available; general molecular DFT and other periodic materials remain unvalidated.

Atlas homeMethod mapBrowse by equationRun hydrogenic / He examplesRunnable examples and next plansPrimary sources and documentation

Three choices to keep separate

Physical model and approximation

HF, KS-DFT, MP2, CI or CC: which many-electron states and energies are approximated?

Representation and discretization

Basis, grid, pseudopotential and k sampling: how is the model made finite?

Equation solver

Eigensolvers, SCF, mixing and DIIS: how accurately is the chosen discrete problem solved?

SCF convergence, basis convergence and physical adequacy are distinct checks. Representative equations use atomic units (ℏ = m_e = e = 4πε₀ = 1). Finite molecules and periodic solids also require different boundaries.

Electronic-structure models

  • Schrodinger eigenproblems
  • Hartree–Fock
  • Kohn–Sham density functional theory / DFT
  • LDA, GGA and hybrid functionals

Representations and nonlinear iteration

  • Electronic-structure basis sets
  • Self-consistent field iteration / SCF
  • Pulay / DIIS acceleration
  • Coulomb and Hartree potentials
  • Pseudopotentials and PAW
  • Periodic electronic structure and k-point sampling
  • Band symmetry groups and irreducible representations

Many-electron correlation

  • MP2 perturbation theory
  • Configuration interaction / CI
  • Coupled cluster / CCSD(T)
  • CASSCF and multireference methods
  • Quantum Monte Carlo
  • DMRG and tensor networks

Excitations and time evolution

  • Time-dependent density functional theory / TDDFT
  • Born–Oppenheimer molecular dynamics / BOMD
  • Car–Parrinello molecular dynamics / CPMD

Schrodinger eigenproblems

The common starting point is a many-electron eigenproblem at fixed nuclear positions. We use nonrelativistic Born–Oppenheimer theory and atomic units, separating electronic energy E_el from nuclear repulsion E_NN. R_A and Z_A denote nuclear positions and charges; r_ij is an electron–electron distance.

For one electron the pair-repulsion sum vanishes; hydrogenic energies E_n = −Z²/(2n²) provide references. The many-electron wavefunction depends on all electronic coordinates and spins, unlike the individual three-dimensional orbitals in HF or KS.

Uniform radial-grid tests of isolated hydrogenic 1s, 2s, 2p and 3d states; not a direct general many-electron Schrödinger solver. Fixed inputs, code and measured checks

Kohn–Sham density functional theory / DFT

Here DFT means density functional theory, rather than the discrete Fourier transform. Within the Hohenberg–Kohn ground-state framework, Kohn–Sham theory represents the density using auxiliary noninteracting orbitals. State the spin convention for occupations f_i and enforce their sum N.

T_s is the auxiliary kinetic energy and E_H the classical Coulomb energy. E_xc includes exchange, correlation and the difference between interacting kinetic energy and T_s. Updating density to potential and orbitals back to density produces the nonlinear SCF problem.

The representative local KS equation below assumes a differentiable density functional. Distinguish generalized KS treatments of nonlocal hybrid exchange and orbital-dependent meta-GGAs.

Band symmetry groups and irreducible representations

A structural space group includes translations, rotations, mirrors, inversion and their combinations. Band classification must use the symmetries actually preserved by the Hamiltonian, including magnetic order, spin–orbit coupling (SOC) and external fields.

A Seitz operation g = {R|τ} maps position to Rr + τ. With lattice translations T as a normal subgroup, G/T is the crystal point group. At each k, the little group G_k retains operations taking Rk back to k modulo a reciprocal vector K. Its little co-group G_k/T is distinct from the full crystal point group.

Read little-group irreps and degeneracies

Symmetries act within the Bloch-state space associated with k. Irreducible small representations classify bands. Their dimensions constrain symmetry-required multiplicities; accidental coincidence and antiunitary pairing are additional possibilities. Nearly equal energies alone do not identify an irrep.

Little groups change between high-symmetry points, lines and planes. Compatibility relations track representation branching and band connectivity. For a simple symmorphic mirror line without SOC, mirror eigenvalues +1 and −1 label distinct sectors that cannot hybridize while that symmetry is preserved.

Screw axes, glide planes and nonsymmorphic groups

Screw and glide operations include fractional translations. Bloch phases matter, particularly at zone boundaries, so ordinary crystal-point-group character tables are insufficient. Use little-group small representations or equivalent projective little-co-group representations with their factor systems.

Nonsymmorphic symmetry can constrain degeneracies and connectivity. It does not imply that every band is degenerate at every k: specify the group, k, spin and time-reversal conditions.

SOC, double groups, time reversal and Kramers pairs

Spin-1/2 SOC requires spinors that change sign under a 2π rotation, hence double-valued representations of double groups. Time reversal Θ is antiunitary with Θ² = −1 for electrons. Time reversal alone generally pairs k with −k; Kramers degeneracy at the same k is guaranteed at time-reversal-invariant momenta (TRIM), where 2k is reciprocal.

In the usual nonmagnetic spin-1/2 setting with both inversion P and time reversal Θ, PΘ preserves each k and squares to −1, producing double degeneracy at each k. This conclusion cannot be transferred unchanged to a noncentrosymmetric system. Spinless Θ² = +1 models also do not satisfy these Kramers assumptions.

Magnetic order may break time reversal or retain only its combination with a spatial operation. Magnetic space groups and antiunitary corepresentations require separate treatment. Reassess symmetry settings whenever SOC or magnetic state changes.

Hydrogenic atoms and helium: runnable validation examples

From analytic references to self-consistency: run hydrogenic radial equations and closed-shell HF / exchange-only LDA for helium, with measured errors and explicit limits.

ewald.title: Ewald summation
ewald.html:
Ewald summation

Ewald summation evaluates periodic Coulomb interactions through complementary real- and reciprocal-space sums. It defines a different boundary-value problem from simply truncating 1/r at a finite radius.

Problem and representative equations

Consider point charges qᵢ in a neutral, triply periodic cell. Set rᵢⱼₙ=rᵢ−rⱼ+n, cell volume V, splitting parameter α>0 and reciprocal vector k. S(k) is the charge structure factor. The energy below uses unit Coulomb prefactor, omits k=0 and assumes a conducting macroscopic boundary. The prime excludes only i=j,n=0.

S(k)=∑jqjeik⋅rj,E=12∑i,j,n′qiqjerfc⁡(αrijn)rijn+2πV∑k≠0e−k2/(4α2)k2∣S(k)∣2−απ∑iqi2.\begin{aligned}S(\mathbf k)&=\sum_jq_j e^{i\mathbf k\cdot\mathbf r_j},\\E&=\frac12\sum_{i,j,\mathbf n}^{\prime}q_iq_j\frac{\operatorname{erfc}(\alpha r_{ij\mathbf n})}{r_{ij\mathbf n}}+\frac{2\pi}{V}\sum_{\mathbf k\ne0}\frac{e^{-k^2/(4\alpha^2)}}{k^2}|S(\mathbf k)|^2-\frac{\alpha}{\sqrt\pi}\sum_iq_i^2.\end{aligned}S(k)E​=j∑​qj​eik⋅rj​,=21​i,j,n∑′​qi​qj​rijn​erfc(αrijn​)​+V2π​k=0∑​k2e−k2/(4α2)​∣S(k)∣2−π​α​i∑​qi2​.​

Algorithm

Accumulate screened real-space pairs and Gaussian-damped reciprocal modes, then subtract the self energy. Restore the same Coulomb prefactor to every term in dimensional units. Changing α redistributes work between sums but cannot change their converged total. Derive forces from the same energy convention.

Conditions and pitfalls

A net-charged cell requires an additional convention such as a compensating background. Specify potential gauge, surface term, periodic self images and molecular exclusions separately. A periodic gravitational Poisson solve changes the kernel/sign and mean-density treatment; it is not the same calculation.

The companion release keeps an asymmetric neutral eight-charge cubic cell, triply periodic with tin-foil boundaries. It separates the direct-Ewald splitting parameter, real-image and reciprocal-cube cutoffs, using a separately implemented heat-kernel theta integral as a reference. It does not extend to charged backgrounds or slabs.

What to check

For a small neutral configuration, increase both cutoffs independently and test α independence. Compare forces with finite differences of energy, and check translation invariance and net force. Agreement between two unconverged sums is not independent validation.

Historical and companion inputs, criteria and results are retained separately. The companion checks energy and every particle force, refinement of the reference integral itself, translations, particle ordering, net force and energy differences individually; a deliberately truncated control is distinct from a converged reference.

pme.title: Particle mesh Ewald / PME
pme.html:
Particle mesh Ewald / PME

PME transfers the reciprocal Ewald calculation to a mesh and uses FFTs. Distinguish the original Lagrange-interpolation PME from the later B-spline construction of SPME.

Problem and representative equations

For a neutral triply periodic Coulomb system, Qₘ is charge assigned to mesh point xₘ using weights Wₘ. The reciprocal operator Ĝₕ includes Ewald screening, mesh conventions and interpolation corrections. This schematic describes only the reciprocal contribution; real-space and self terms remain necessary.

Qm=∑iqiWm(ri),ϕh=Fh−1 ⁣[G^h FhQ].Q_{\mathbf m}=\sum_iq_iW_{\mathbf m}(\mathbf r_i),\qquad\phi_h=\mathcal F_h^{-1}\!\left[\widehat G_h\,\mathcal F_h Q\right].Qm​=i∑​qi​Wm​(ri​),ϕh​=Fh−1​[Gh​Fh​Q].

Algorithm

Assign charges with local Lagrange polynomials, transform the mesh, apply the reciprocal convolution and transform back. Specify the differentiation and particle-gather rules together. A mesh-interpolated field and the derivative of the discrete energy need not give identical forces.

Conditions and pitfalls

Separate mesh resolution, interpolation order, Ewald cutoffs and force differentiation in error studies. State FFT normalization, k=0 treatment and units. The usual O(N log N) description assumes an appropriate mesh-growth regime and is not an accuracy guarantee.

The linked implementation adopts smooth PME with B-spline analytical energy gradients. It does not implement or validate the original 1993 Lagrange-interpolation PME; the original PME equations, sources and applicability remain distinct from this implemented variant.

What to check

Use a converged direct Ewald calculation for the identical neutral cell. Vary mesh size, interpolation order and screening; measure RMS/maximum energy and force errors and sensitivity to common translations. A gravity-PM test does not validate PME.

The companion varies mesh size, B-spline order and common translation for the same neutral periodic charges, comparing against converged direct Ewald and a separately implemented theta integral. The direct-Ewald comparison shares real-space/self terms, so agreement there alone is not independent validation of the entire energy.

Check fixed inputs: separate scoped releases

Check each example’s inputs, observables, diagnostic definitions and scope. What a passing check establishes depends on its acceptance criteria and differs from a general mathematical guarantee. Historical inputs, measurements and criteria are preserved.

Mesh/order convergence of B-spline smooth PME

Computation for a fixed target

A small smooth-PME example assigns charge with B-splines and evaluates the Ewald reciprocal contribution by FFT.

Finite-mesh aliasing permits nonzero net force for this energy-gradient variant; that diagnostic is reported. No exact momentum conservation, long MD, original PME, optimized P³M or slab validation is claimed.

spme.title: Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME
spme.html:
Smooth particle mesh Ewald / SPME

SPME approximates Ewald structure factors using smooth cardinal B-splines. Treat it as a specific interpolation-and-force construction rather than a synonym for every PME implementation.

Problem and representative equations

Let uᵢ be particle coordinates in mesh units and Mₚ a cardinal B-spline of order p, not degree p. The product below is the local tensor assignment in three dimensions. Fourier structure factors require a correction for the spline response.

Qmxmymz=∑iqi∏d∈{x,y,z}Mp(uid−md),deg⁡Mp=p−1.Q_{m_xm_ym_z}=\sum_iq_i\prod_{d\in\{x,y,z\}}M_p(u_{id}-m_d),\qquad \deg M_p=p-1.Qmx​my​mz​​=i∑​qi​d∈{x,y,z}∏​Mp​(uid​−md​),degMp​=p−1.

Algorithm

Spread charge over p neighboring mesh points in each direction, evaluate a corrected reciprocal mesh energy by FFT, and obtain forces using derivatives of the assignment in analytical differentiation. Record the spline order and mesh together with whether differentiation is analytical or in Fourier space.

Conditions and pitfalls

Smooth assignment alone does not guarantee both energy consistency and exact net-force cancellation. Ewald neutrality, boundary and self-term conventions still apply. Comparisons with original PME should control error tolerance and differentiation rules, not merely the number of mesh points.

The companion also uses analytical energy gradients with B-spline orders 4/6. Discrete energy–force consistency, common-translation mesh effects and net force are separate observables. Finite-mesh aliasing generally permits nonzero net force; exact momentum conservation is not claimed.

What to check

Measure force errors against the same converged Ewald reference and check energy finite differences. Report common-translation mesh effects and total force separately. Ensure real-space truncation is not hiding the reciprocal-space convergence trend.

The design compares 16³/24³/40³ meshes and several common translations against matching direct-Ewald and independent theta references. It separates partition of unity/charge, energy differences, RMS/maximum force errors and real-space truncation; it supplies no evidence for long MD or original PME.

Check fixed inputs: separate scoped releases

Check each example’s inputs, observables, diagnostic definitions and scope. What a passing check establishes depends on its acceptance criteria and differs from a general mathematical guarantee. Historical inputs, measurements and criteria are preserved.

Mesh/order convergence of B-spline smooth PME

Computation for a fixed target

A small smooth-PME example assigns charge with B-splines and evaluates the Ewald reciprocal contribution by FFT.

Finite-mesh aliasing permits nonzero net force for this energy-gradient variant; that diagnostic is reported. No exact momentum conservation, long MD, original PME, optimized P³M or slab validation is claimed.

slab-ewald.title: Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald
slab-ewald.html:
Slab electrostatics and 2D-periodic Ewald

Interfaces often require periodicity in two directions and isolation in the normal direction. Elongating a triply periodic cell is not identical to evaluating the genuinely two-periodic Green function.

Problem and representative equations

For a neutral cell of volume V, normal z and unit Coulomb prefactor, the Yeh–Berkowitz correction adds a dipole contribution to a specified three-periodic Ewald baseline. Its coordinate derivative gives the normal force correction. The formula assumes neutrality and a conducting-boundary 3D reference.

Mz=∑iqizi,ΔE=2πVMz2,ΔFi,z=−4πVqiMz.M_z=\sum_iq_i z_i,\qquad \Delta E=\frac{2\pi}{V}M_z^2,\qquad \Delta F_{i,z}=-\frac{4\pi}{V}q_iM_z.Mz​=i∑​qi​zi​,ΔE=V2π​Mz2​,ΔFi,z​=−V4π​qi​Mz​.

Algorithm

Place slabs in an elongated cell with vacuum, converge the 3D sums, and add the dipole correction. Increase the vacuum height to assess residual image interactions. At finite vacuum height, this is not a claim of exact equivalence to a fully two-periodic summation.

Conditions and pitfalls

Charged slabs, other external dielectric conditions, electrodes and imposed fields require additional formulations. Keep self and k=0 conventions distinct from this correction. Neutral-cell M_z is invariant under an origin shift; net charge destroys that property.

What to check

Use neutral charge pairs or a dipole layer and vary vacuum height independently of reciprocal/mesh cutoffs. Compare with an independent two-periodic reference when available, and finite-difference the energy for normal forces. Agreement with an uncorrected 3D calculation cannot establish zero slab error.

Publication scope and related entries
